title: Al-Ma'idah
label: Plain-English commentary
intro:
Surah Al-Ma'idah, "The Table Spread", is a Madinan surah of one hundred and twenty verses. It was revealed late, after the Prophet ﷺ had settled in Madinah and the community had grown into a state with treaties, boundaries and a public life. Several reports place it among the very last surahs to come down: At-Tirmidhi recorded that 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said the last surahs revealed were Surat Al-Ma'idah and Surat Al-Fath, and At-Tirmidhi graded that report Hasan, Gharib. Al-Hakim collected a similar narration in his Mustadrak and called it Sahih by the criteria of the two Shaykhs. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said that the last surah revealed was "When there comes the help of Allah and the Conquest" [110:1]. Al-Hakim also narrated from Jubayr bin Nufayr that he performed Hajj and visited 'A'ishah, who asked him whether he read Al-Ma'idah. When he said yes, she said it was the last surah to be revealed and that whatever permissible matters are found in it should be treated as permissible and whatever impermissible matters are found in it should be treated as impermissible. Imam Ahmad recorded a version in which Jubayr added that he asked 'A'ishah about the conduct of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and she answered, "The Qur'an." An-Nasa'i also recorded this. The practical lesson drawn from this is that the surah is a closing word on law and obligation: a believer's life is a regulated life, and even where he is free to act, he accepts the supremacy and Lordship of Allah and makes himself subject to regulation.

The name Al-Ma'idah comes from the table spread with food that the disciples of 'Isa (Jesus) asked for, an event the surah itself narrates. The surah's central concern is covenant and obligation: what Allah has permitted, what He has forbidden, and the duty of those who claim faith to honour their treaties, their rituals and their trusts. It opens with a command to believers to fulfil their obligations, and it closes with the scene of the Day of Resurrection when 'Isa (Jesus) is asked about what his people did. Between these two points it lays down food laws, rules of Hajj and Ihram, the sanctity of the Sacred Month and the symbols of Allah, the penalties for hunting in Ihram, the obligation of justice even toward enemies, the prohibition of helping one another in sin, the laws of wudu and tayammum, the ruling on wine and gambling, the command to obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, the duties of witnesses, the stories of the two sons of Adam, of Musa (Moses) and the Children of Israel, of the Sabbath breakers, of the table that was sent down, and of the disciples. It is a surah of law and of history, and it keeps returning to one theme: a covenant taken and then either kept or broken.

### When it was revealed

The material places the surah in Madinah, after the Hijrah and after the community had become responsible for a public order. Its laws presuppose a people who travel for Hajj, who hunt, who trade, who marry, who judge disputes and who live alongside Jews and Christians. The opening verses speak of Ihram, of the Sacred House, of garlands on sacrificial animals and of hunting, all of which belong to a community already performing Hajj. The report of 'A'ishah, that it was the last surah revealed, gives the surah the character of a final review of obligations: whatever permissible matters are found in it are to be treated as permissible and whatever impermissible matters are found in it are to be treated as impermissible.

### What the surah covers

The first passage commands believers to fulfil their obligations, declares lawful all beasts of cattle except what is announced, forbids hunting while in Ihram, and forbids violating the sanctity of the symbols of Allah, the Sacred Month, the sacrificial animal, the garlands and the people coming to the Sacred House. It then commands justice even toward those who once stopped the believers from the Sacred Mosque, and it commands helping one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa while forbidding help in sin and transgression. The next passage explains the lawful and unlawful beasts in detail, the ruling on a fetus found in a slaughtered animal, and the exception for one forced by necessity without wilful disobedience. The surah then turns to wudu, tayammum, and the prohibition of wine and gambling, to the command to obey Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and to the duty of witnesses to be just. The story of the two sons of Adam is told as a warning against envy and murder. The story of Musa (Moses) and the Children of Israel follows, with the breaking of the Sabbath, the sending down of the table, and the request of the disciples. The surah addresses the People of the Book, distinguishes those who believe from those who turn away, and returns again and again to the theme of covenant: the covenant of the Children of Israel, the covenant of the Christians, and the covenant of the believers. It ends with the scene of the Day of Resurrection and the question put to 'Isa (Jesus) about what his people did.

### Its virtues

The surah carries a special weight in the reports. At-Tirmidhi recorded the statement of 'Abdullah bin 'Amr about it being among the last revealed, graded Hasan, Gharib. Al-Hakim collected a similar narration and called it Sahih by the criteria of the two Shaykhs. 'A'ishah's instruction to Jubayr bin Nufayr, to treat its permissible matters as permissible and its impermissible matters as impermissible because it was the last surah revealed, is the most direct statement of its authority in matters of law. Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Abdur-Rahman bin Mahdi related that Mu'awiyah bin Salih added the statement that when Jubayr asked 'A'ishah about the conduct of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ she answered, "The Qur'an." An-Nasa'i also recorded it. The surah is also connected to the practice of Hajj: the Prophet ﷺ, when he intended to perform Hajj, spent the night at Dhul-Hulayfah, which is also called Wadi Al-'Aqiq, and in the morning made rounds with his wives, performed Ghusl, applied perfume, prayed two Rak'ahs, then garlanded the Hady and announced aloud his intention to perform Hajj and 'Umrah. The Prophet's Hady at that time consisted of plenty of camels, more than sixty, among the best and healthiest animals.

### How it connects to the previous surah

Surah An-Nisa' before it deals with family law, inheritance, orphans, women, and the People of the Book, and it too returns to the theme of covenant and to the question of obedience. Al-Ma'idah takes up the same themes at a higher level of public obligation: where An-Nisa' speaks of the household and the clan, Al-Ma'idah speaks of the community as a whole, of treaties between peoples, of the symbols of religion, of Hajj and of justice in the public square. The closing verses of An-Nisa' speak of the Book and of those who are given a share of it, and Al-Ma'idah opens by demanding that the believers fulfil their obligations, as if to say that the law given in the previous surah is now to be carried out in full.

### In short

- Al-Ma'idah is a Madinan surah of one hundred and twenty verses, revealed late and treated in the reports as one of the last surahs to come down.
- Its subject is covenant and obligation: food laws, Hajj and Ihram, wudu and tayammum, wine and gambling, justice, and the stories of the prophets and the People of the Book.
- It commands believers to fulfil their obligations, to help one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa, and not to help one another in sin and transgression.
- It carries a special authority in matters of law, expressed in 'A'ishah's instruction to treat its permissible and impermissible matters as final.
- It follows Surah An-Nisa' and raises the same themes of covenant and obedience to the level of the whole community.

1.text:
This verse opens Surah Al-Ma'idah with a command to the believers: "O believers! Honour your obligations." It then declares that all grazing livestock has been made lawful to eat, except what will be announced later in the surah and except hunting while on pilgrimage. It closes with the reminder that Allah commands what He wills. The verse therefore does three things at once: it calls the believers to keep their covenants, it opens the food laws of the surah, and it asserts that the permission and the prohibition both come from Allah's will.

The setting is Madinah, after the Hijrah, when the community had treaties with neighbouring tribes and was responsible for a public order. The verse speaks to people who already have obligations to keep: covenants with Allah, covenants with other people, and the limits Allah has set in the religion. 'Abdullah bin Mas'ud advised that when one hears "O you who believe," one should pay full attention, for it is either a righteous matter being ordained or an evil thing being forbidden. Khaythamah said that everything in the Qur'an that reads "O you who believe" reads in the Tawrah as "O you who are in need." The verse is therefore a call to attention as much as a command.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers!"** is the address that opens many of the legal passages of the Qur'an. It marks the verse as a command to those who have already accepted faith, not a general announcement to all mankind. The material notes that this address appears repeatedly in the surah and that each time it introduces either an obligation or a prohibition.

**"Honour your obligations"** translates the command to fulfil the covenants. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said that "obligations" here means treaties. Ibn Jarir mentioned that there is a consensus for this view, and he added that it refers to treaties such as the alliances they used to conduct. 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas commented that it refers to the covenants, meaning what Allah permitted, prohibited, ordained and set limits for in the Qur'an, and that the believers must not commit treachery or break the covenants. Ad-Dahhak said that it refers to what Allah has permitted and what He has prohibited, and that Allah took the covenant from those who proclaim faith in the Prophet ﷺ and the Book to fulfil the obligations He ordered for them in the permissible and the impermissible. Allah emphasised this command by referring to those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification and sever what Allah commanded to be joined [13:25].

**"All grazing livestock has been made lawful to you"** refers to camels, cows and sheep, as Al-Hasan, Qatadah and several others stated. Ibn Jarir said that this explanation conforms to the meaning of "beasts of cattle" that the Arabs had. The permission is general and covers the animals the Arabs were familiar with as livestock.

**"except what is hereby announced to you"** refers to the specific circumstances that prohibit some of these animals, which are announced in the following verses. 'Ali bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the flesh of dead animals, blood and the meat of swine. Qatadah gave a narrower reading: carrion, and animals slaughtered without the name of Allah spoken over them. It appears, and Allah knows best, that the verse refers to the detailed list given later in the surah, for although the animals mentioned are types of permissible cattle, they become impermissible under the circumstances specified there. The verse also mentions what is sacrificed on stone altars, which is not permissible because it can no longer be slaughtered properly.

**"and hunting while on pilgrimage"** prohibits hunting wild beasts while in the state of Ihram. Some scholars held that the broad meaning of "cattle" also takes in wild animals of the same kind, such as gazelles, wild oxen and wild donkeys, alongside the domestic animals. Allah made the exceptions mentioned above and prohibited hunting wild beasts while in Ihram. It was also reported that the meaning here is that all types of cattle were allowed in all circumstances except what was excluded for the one hunting game while in Ihram. The exception for one forced by necessity, without wilful disobedience and not transgressing, is given later, and Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful in such cases.

**"Indeed, Allah commands what He wills"** closes the verse by asserting that the permission and the prohibition both belong to Allah. The verse means that just as all cattle were allowed in all conditions and circumstances, hunting game in Ihram is forbidden, for this is the decision of Allah, Who is the Most Wise in all that He commands and forbids.

### Why the verse opens the surah

The verse is placed first because the surah is a surah of obligations, and the first obligation is to keep the covenant. The food laws that follow are themselves part of that covenant: a believer's life is a regulated life, and even where he is free to act, he accepts the supremacy and Lordship of Allah and makes himself subject to regulation. The verse also connects to the previous surah, An-Nisa', which spoke of the People of the Book and of those given a share of the Book. Al-Ma'idah opens by demanding that the believers fulfil their obligations, as if to say that the law given before is now to be carried out in full.

### The ruling on the fetus in the womb

Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, among others, took this verse as the basis for allowing the meat of a fetus found dead in the belly of a slaughtered mother. A report in the Sunan collections of Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, passed on through Abu Sa'id, describes people asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about such a fetus. He told them to eat it if they wished, since its slaughter is complete once its mother has been slaughtered. At-Tirmidhi graded this report Hasan. Abu Dawud also recorded a saying from Jabir bin 'Abdullah that the proper slaughter of the unborn young is accomplished by the slaughter of the mother. Only Abu Dawud collected that second report.

### The sanctity of the symbols and the Sacred Month

The next verse, 5:2, forbids the believers to violate the sanctity of the symbols of Allah, the Sacred Month, the animals brought as offerings, the garlands on them, and those travelling to the Sacred House. Ibn 'Abbas said that the symbols of Allah are the rituals of Hajj. Mujahid said that As-Safa and Al-Marwah and the sacrificial animal are the symbols of Allah. It was also said that the symbols are what Allah prohibited. The Sacred Month is to be respected and honoured, and fighting during it is a great transgression [2:217]. Al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih that Abu Bakrah reported the Prophet ﷺ speaking during the Farewell Hajj. He said that time has returned to the form it had when Allah created the heavens and the earth. The year has twelve months, and four of them are sacred. Three come one after another, and the fourth stands alone, a month of the tribe of Mudar. The material reads this report as proof that the sanctity of these months continues until the end of time.

### The Hady and the garlands

The command not to abandon the practice of bringing the Hady to the Sacred House is a form of honouring the symbols of Allah. The garlands on the necks of the animals distinguish them from other cattle, so that it is known that these animals are intended to be offered as Hady at the Ka'bah, and those who might intend harm to them would refrain. Those who see the Hady might be encouraged to imitate the ritual, and he who calls to a type of guidance earns rewards equal to the rewards of those who follow his lead, without decrease in their own rewards. When the Prophet ﷺ intended to perform Hajj, he spent the night at Dhul-Hulayfah, which is also called Wadi Al-'Aqiq. In the morning he made rounds with his wives, who were nine at that time, performed Ghusl, applied perfume, prayed two Rak'ahs, then garlanded the Hady and announced aloud his intention to perform Hajj and 'Umrah. The Prophet's Hady at that time consisted of plenty of camels, more than sixty, among the best and healthiest animals.

### Justice even toward enemies

The verse's context includes a command that hatred for some people, who once stopped the believers from the Sacred Mosque, must not push the believers into transgression. Believers are to help one another in Al-Birr and At-Taqwa, and not in sin and transgression. The material gives a setting for this. Zayd bin Aslam reported that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions were near Al-Hudaybiyyah when idolators had blocked them from the House, which weighed heavily on them. Later, some idolators passed them heading out for 'Umrah, and some Companions wanted to block them in return. Then this verse came down. Ibn 'Abbas and others explained that "Shana'an" means enmity and hatred. The lesson drawn is that justice is owed to everyone in every situation, even to people one dislikes.

### In short

- The verse commands believers to honour their obligations, which Ibn 'Abbas and others explained as treaties and covenants.
- It declares all grazing livestock lawful except what is announced later and except hunting while on pilgrimage.
- It asserts that Allah commands what He wills, so both permission and prohibition come from Him.
- It is followed by commands about the symbols of Allah, the Sacred Month, the Hady and the garlands, and by the duty of justice even toward enemies.

2.text:
This verse gives the believers two instructions that work together. The first is to protect the things Allah has made sacred: "O believers! Do not violate Allah’s rituals", the sacred months, the animals brought as offerings, the garlands hung on them, and the people travelling to the Sacred House to seek their Lord's favour. The second is to refuse to answer an injustice with another injustice. The verse says that the hatred of a people who once blocked the believers from the Sacred Mosque must not drive them into transgression. Instead, believers must help one another in what is good and God-fearing, and never in sin and aggression. The verse ends with the reminder to be mindful of Allah, because His punishment is severe.

The verse follows directly from the one before it, which asked believers to honour their obligations. This verse spells out two parts of that obligation: respect for the signs of Allah, and justice even toward enemies. It belongs to the same period as the events of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, when the Muslims were stopped from performing 'Umrah, and to the period after, when some of them wanted to take revenge.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers!"** is the same address as in the previous verse. It turns to people who have already accepted faith and asks them to act on that acceptance.

**"Do not violate Allah’s rituals"** translates the Arabic word sha'ā'ir, which the material explains as the plural of sha'īrah, a mark, sign or symbol. The things called sha'ā'ir are visible acts that point to something beyond themselves. Ibn 'Abbas said they are the rites of Hajj. Mujahid said they are As-Safa and Al-Marwah and the sacrificial animal. Other reports give a wider meaning. Al-Hasan al-Basri and 'Ata' are quoted as giving the clearest and most general reading: the sha'ā'ir of Allah are all the obligations whose limits the Shari'ah has set. Al-Jassas is said to have treated their words as a summary of all the other readings. On that reading, violating the signs of Allah has three forms. One is to abandon the obligations altogether. A second is to keep some of them and drop others. A third is to cross the limits that have been set. The verse forbids all three. The material also points out that the Qur'an gives the same instruction in another place: whoever exalts the signs of Allah shows the fear of Allah in the heart [22:32].

**"the sacred months"** refers to the four months during which fighting was forbidden: Dhul-Qa'dah, Dhul-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab. The material adds that the rule against fighting in these months was later changed. Some reports say the verse on the garlands was abrogated, and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said the same about another verse of the surah. The scholars the material quotes agree that the ban on fighting in the sacred months was abrogated. Even so, the sacred months remain a reason to avoid sin, as 2:217 makes clear when it calls fighting in them a great transgression.

**"the sacrificial animals"** are the Hady, animals brought to the Sacred House to be slaughtered. The verse forbids preventing them from reaching the Sacred Area, and forbids seizing them. The material notes that verse 5:3 lists the sacrifice made on stone altars, An-Nusub, as forbidden, because such an animal can no longer be slaughtered properly. The material also forbids using such an animal for riding or milking when it has been set aside as an offering. Muqatil bin Hayyan said that "do not breach their sanctity" is the meaning of the instruction about the garlands.

**"the garlands"** are the markings placed on the animals' necks to show that they are offerings. The material records that in the period before Islam people hung animal hair and pelts on themselves when they travelled outside the sacred months, and that the idolaters of the Sacred Area hung tree-stems from the Sacred Area so that they could travel safely. Those garlands are not to be violated.

**"nor those ˹pilgrims˺ on their way to the Sacred House"** protects the people going to the Sacred House. The material says the verse means that no one heading to the House with the intention of seeking Allah's pleasure may be fought, stopped, or frightened away. Mujahid, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and several others took "the bounty of their Lord" to mean trade, which the pilgrims were allowed to carry on during Hajj. Ibn 'Abbas took the word "pleasure" to mean that the pilgrimage itself was done to seek Allah's pleasure. The Sacred Mosque mentioned here is al-Masjid al-Haram at Makkah.

**"seeking their Lord’s bounty and pleasure"** names the purpose of such people. Trade is named as one way of seeking provision, and the intention to please Allah is named as the reason for the journey. The material connects this to a particular man, al-Hutam, who had driven away the livestock of Madinah. The verse came down, and when the Muslims wanted to attack him on his way to the House, they were held back.

**"When pilgrimage has ended, you are allowed to hunt."** The earlier verse banned hunting while in Ihram. This phrase lifts that ban once the pilgrim has left the state of Ihram. The material says the command is a permission and not a requirement. It also notes that the rule applies after leaving the Sanctuary, so that hunting inside the Sacred Area remains forbidden.

**"Do not let the hatred of a people who once barred you from the Sacred Mosque provoke you to transgress."** This is the central instruction of the verse. The reference is to the people of Makkah who stopped the believers at Hudaybiyyah. The material says that the Muslims returned from Hudaybiyyah sad and angry. Now that they were in a position of strength, some of them wanted to repay that treatment by stopping the Makkans from reaching the House. The verse forbids this because it is injustice, and Islam does not allow injustice to be avenged with more injustice. The material treats this as a rule that holds in every circumstance.

**"Cooperate with one another in goodness and righteousness"** is the positive instruction. The Arabic words are Al-Birr, which the material says means doing good deeds, and At-Taqwa, which means keeping away from what is evil. Ibn Jarir and others explained that believers must help one another in good actions and in avoiding what is wrong.

**"and do not cooperate in sin and transgression."** The material defines sin, ithm, as disobedience in matters of rights and in acts of worship alike. Transgression, 'udwan, means crossing the limits set by Allah, which is injustice and aggression. Ibn Jarir put it this way: sin is leaving aside what Allah has ordained, and transgression is going past the bounds He has set, both in religion and in how a person deals with himself and with others.

**"And be mindful of Allah."** This is the closing command. The material explains that taqwā means fearing Allah in what He has commanded and forbidden. It makes the ground of all the earlier instructions clear: a believer keeps the covenant, respects the signs and acts justly because of the fear of Allah.

**"Surely Allah is severe in punishment."** The verse ends with a warning. Those who abstain from what Allah has commanded will face His punishment, and the material understands this as the reason to avoid the transgressions just described.

### The story behind the verse

The material gives a detailed background, and it is worth knowing because it shows what the verse was addressing. In the sixth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ set out with more than a thousand Companions to perform 'Umrah. The people of Makkah refused to let them enter and imposed hard conditions in a treaty: the Muslims were to return that year and come back the next year without weapons, to stay only three days and to leave after 'Umrah. The Muslims accepted this out of obedience, and they performed the missed 'Umrah in the seventh year. The treaty left seeds of anger among the Companions.

The material then tells of al-Hutam, whose name is given as Hatim ibn Hind, one of the chiefs of Makkah. Some reports name him as Sharih ibn Dubay'ah al-Kindi. He came to Madinah to trade, then came to the Prophet ﷺ claiming he wished to become Muslim, but he said he had chiefs whose agreement he needed. The Prophet ﷺ had already told his Companions that a man was coming who would speak with the words of the devil. When the man left, the Prophet ﷺ described him as coming with the face of a disbeliever and going away with the steps of a traitor. The man then drove off the camels that were grazing outside Madinah. In the seventh year, when the Muslims were going to perform the missed 'Umrah, they heard someone chanting the talbiyah at a distance. It was al-Hutam, with the stolen animals wearing garlands as offerings. Some Companions wanted to attack him and take back the animals. Ibn Jarir and al-Suddi, quoting 'Ikrimah, related that the verse was revealed about this man and this moment, and it forbade the Muslims to act against him.

The material also gives a second setting, which it presents as the later one. After the conquest of Makkah in the eighth year, the Makkans were free and kept their pagan practices of Hajj and 'Umrah. Some Companions wanted to take revenge for Hudaybiyyah by stopping them. The verse was used to forbid this. The material explains that, whatever the setting, the lesson is the same.

### What the verse says about hunting after Ihram

The material explains that the first verse of the surah banned hunting during Ihram. Here the limit of that prohibition is set. Ihram ends, and the hunting that was forbidden becomes lawful again. Some scholars took this as an instruction that lifts a prohibition, which is different from a new command. The material also points to the rule that hunting within the Sacred Area stays forbidden, because the permission applies only to pilgrims who leave the Sanctuary.

One reading takes the permission as plain, and another reads it as the end of a state of prohibition, so that the believer is free again. None of the readings treats the permission as a duty.

### The disagreement about abrogation

The material contains more than one view about whether parts of this verse were changed. One reading says that the Makkan pagans falsely claimed that the verse about sacred things was still binding, and it points to the verse of repudiation in Surat At-Tawbah as the one that settled the matter. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said the verse on the garlands was abrogated, along with another verse of the surah. The consensus cited about the sacred months is that the ban on fighting in them was lifted. The material presents these as different claims and does not reduce them to one settled answer.

### Justice toward enemies

The material is clear that the verse forbids revenge that wrongs people who have done nothing new. The Qur'an, the material says, teaches that friend and foe are to be weighed on the same scale of justice [5:8], which is nearer to piety. Believers are commanded to do justice as an obligation, however hostile the enemy and however great the harm suffered. The material presents this as one of the distinctive qualities of Islam, which does not answer one wrong with another but chooses justice in return. Another reading explains the verse in the same way: the people who had blocked the believers were not to be blocked in return, and the pilgrims of one clan were not to be attacked because of the crimes of another.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded a report from Zayd bin Aslam about the setting at Al-Hudaybiyyah, which the material also gives. The Companions wanted to block a group of idolaters on their way to 'Umrah, because the idolaters had blocked them, and then this verse came down. Ibn 'Abbas and others explained that "Shana'an" means enmity and hatred. The lesson is that hatred must not cause injustice, because justice is owed in every situation.

### Helping one another in righteousness

This part of the verse has a broad reach in the material. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others took it as a rule that governs the whole community. Believers help one another in what is righteous and God-fearing, and they must not help one another in sin and aggression.

The material draws a clear limit. The verse does not say that help should go only to fellow Muslims and not to others. It makes righteousness and the fear of Allah the basis of cooperation, and so it applies also among Muslims. Help must not be given to a Muslim brother who is acting against the truth or moving toward injustice. Instead, the believer should hold his hand back from wrong, because that is the truest help. A report found in the Sahih collections of al-Bukhari and Muslim, through Anas, says that the Prophet ﷺ told his Companions to help their brother whether he was just or unjust. They asked how one helps an oppressor. He said: stop him from doing injustice, and that is helping him. Ahmad recorded a similar report, and al-Bukhari recorded it through Hushaym.

The material also gives related reports about the rewards of guidance. A believer who mixes with people and bears their harm with patience earns more reward than one who keeps away from them. Muslim recorded that whoever calls to guidance earns a reward like that of everyone who follows him, without any loss to their reward, and whoever calls to error carries a burden like that of everyone who follows him, without any reduction in their burden. Tabarani is cited for the report that whoever joins an unjust person to help him leaves the fold of Islam. Scholars in the material explain that this is why the righteous of earlier times refused to hold office in the courts of unjust rulers. A further report, which the material introduces with the verse "I will never be a helper for the criminals" [28:17], says that on the Day of Judgment a call will go out for the oppressors and their helpers, even those who only prepared the pens and inkpots of the unjust.

### Cooperation as the order of the world

The material gives a long reflection on the verse's second half. It argues that human life depends on cooperation. No one can grow, process and transport his own food, make his own clothes, or build his own house. Each person needs hundreds and thousands of others, and this mutual need keeps the world going. The material says that Allah put into each person the inclination and liking for the work for which He created him, so that people take up their work willingly, without legal compulsion, and earn their living through it. The result is that most needs are met for a modest price. The material gives the examples of a hotel meal and a taxi, where the food and the vehicle each bring together the work of many people from many countries.

The material then contrasts this with systems that take the choice of work away from people through force. Such systems, it says, cost the freedom of the people involved and did not prove economical. The same argument holds that cooperation has a darker side. If it is used for theft, robbery, killing and destruction, the same power of cooperation can damage the whole order. For that reason, people in the past formed groups and nations based on ideology and kinship for their own security.

### The formation of separate nations

The material, quoting 'Abd al-Karim al-Shahristani, gives an account of how people came to think of themselves as separate nations. At first, when the population was small, people living in the four directions regarded themselves as four nations. Later, nationalism grew on the basis of lineage, family and tribe. Arabia was organised on this basis, and tribes went to war over these ties. The material says that a similar division of castes still persisted in parts of India. It then describes how modern nations were formed on the basis of region, language and homeland, and how this division also reached the Muslim world.

The material then gives the Qur'an's answer. The surah an-Nisa' says that all human beings come from one father and one mother. At his last Hajj the Prophet ﷺ declared that no Arab is better than a non-Arab, and no white person is better than a black person. Superiority depends only on taqwā. The Qur'an calls believers brothers [49:10], and it draws the line of kinship at faith rather than blood. Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab were cut off from the Prophet ﷺ, while Bilal from Ethiopia and Suhayb from Byzantium were joined to him. The verse "He it is who created you, then some of you are disbelievers and some are believers" [64:2] is read as the basic division of mankind. The material says that at Badr, Uhud, the Ahzab and Hunayn, close relatives who stayed away from Allah and His Messenger found that their bond had broken.

### Why the verse is a warning about crime

The material adds a practical warning. Those who see a crime and keep silent, or refuse to give true witness when a crime needs to be proven, are helping the criminal. The material says this is a serious sin and a clear disobedience of the command to help one another in righteousness. Ibn Abi Hatim and other reports carry the same warning about helping the unjust. The material also says that real change does not come from parades or training alone. It comes through education in righteousness and the fear of Allah, which is the way to make people promote good and oppose evil.

### In short

- The verse protects the signs of Allah, including the sacred months, the offerings, the garlands and the pilgrims, and forbids all three forms of violating them.
- It forbids revenge against people who once blocked the believers, because injustice must not be answered with injustice.
- It sets righteousness and the fear of Allah as the basis for all cooperation, including cooperation among Muslims.
- The material links it to the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, the case of al-Hutam, and the wider principle of justice toward enemies.
- It ends with a warning: be mindful of Allah, because His punishment is severe.

3.text:
This verse is the list of what is forbidden to eat, and it ends with a message that the material calls one of the most important in the whole Qur'an. It opens: "Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine". It then names the animal that was killed in the name of someone other than Allah, the animal killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or a goring, and the animal half eaten by a predator. It forbids the animal sacrificed on stone altars and the practice of drawing arrows to decide matters. Then the verse turns to the believers and tells them that the disbelievers have given up hope of destroying their faith, that Allah has perfected their religion and completed His favour on them, and that Islam is their way. It ends with a permission: the person who is driven by severe hunger, without any intention to sin, may eat what is otherwise forbidden, because Allah forgives and shows mercy.

The verse sits inside a longer passage about food, oaths, the Hady, and the duties of the believers. The previous verse set out the limits of the sacred months and the pilgrim's obligations, and this verse goes on to the rules for what is lawful to eat. The reports say the verse came down during the Farewell Pilgrimage, on the day of 'Arafah in the tenth year after the Hijrah, which fell on a Friday. The material treats that date as a sign of the completion of the religion, and it is discussed at length in the entry below.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, and swine"** names the three basic prohibitions. Carrion, in Arabic maytah, is an animal that died without being slaughtered, whether from sickness or from natural death. The material says it is harmful to the body and also to character. Blood means blood that flows. The verse refers to flowing blood, as Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id bin Jubayr explained, and the material notes that the Qur'an says the same in 6:145. Liver and spleen are therefore not included, since they are not blood that flows out. Swine means the whole animal, including the fat, since the Arabic word lahm covers the whole flesh of the animal. A report collected by Muslim makes the point clear, through Buraydah bin al-Husayb al-Aslami, who said that the Prophet ﷺ compared a person who plays the dice game with someone who puts his hand into the flesh and blood of swine. If touching is that serious, eating is much worse.

**"what is slaughtered in the name of any other than Allah"** is the ban on sacrifice to anyone but Allah. The material says that when a name other than Allah is spoken over an animal at slaughter, whether an idol, a false god, or a shrine, the meat becomes unlawful, and that the scholars agree on this. Muslim jurists also treat as forbidden an animal that is offered to someone other than Allah, even if the name of Allah is spoken, because the act is still a form of associating partners with Him. Abu Sufyan is reported to have told the Emperor Heraclius that the Prophet ﷺ forbade eating dead animals and blood, which the material cites as a sign of how widely the prohibitions were known.

**"what is killed by strangling, beating, a fall, or by being gored to death"** lists four ways an animal can die without the proper slaughter. Strangling, whether by mistake or on purpose, makes the animal unlawful. A beating with a staff, rod or stone makes the animal unlawful, and the material notes that the people of the time of ignorance used to beat animals and then eat them. A hunter who strikes game with the broad side of an arrow, so that it is killed by the blow and not by the cut, may not eat it. The report of 'Adi bin Hatim says that if the sharp edge hits and wounds the game, it may be eaten. A fall from a height or into a well, or a death from being gored by another animal's horns, also makes the animal unlawful, even if blood is seen to flow.

**"what is partly eaten by a predator unless you slaughter it"** forbids an animal that a lion, leopard, tiger, wolf or dog has attacked and partly eaten, if it then dies. The material says this too was the custom of the pre-Islamic period, which the Qur'an forbade. The exception is found in the phrase "unless you slaughter it". The material explains that an animal in this state that is still alive and moving may be properly slaughtered and then eaten. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id bin Jubayr, al-Hasan al-Basri and as-Suddi all gave this reading, and 'Ali is reported to have said that if the animal still moves a foot or a leg it may be slaughtered and eaten. Rafi' bin Khadij, in a report in the two Sahih collections, asked the Prophet ﷺ whether they could use reeds to slaughter an animal when they had no knives. He said that anything that makes the blood flow may be used, with the name of Allah spoken, but not teeth or claws.

**"and what is sacrificed on altars"** forbids the animal offered on the stone altars, an-nusub, which stood around the Ka'bah. The material notes that there were about three hundred and sixty of them, and that the Arabs of the time of ignorance would slaughter animals before them, sprinkle the blood on the stones and cut up the meat and place it on the altars. The Qur'an forbids this, and it also forbids eating the meat of animals slaughtered near the altars, even where the name of Allah was spoken, because the practice is itself a form of associating partners with Allah.

**"You are also forbidden to draw lots for decisions"** deals with the arrows, al-azlam. The material describes a method in which three arrows were used: one marked "do", one marked "do not", and one blank. The blank arrow meant the draw had to be repeated until one of the others came out. Some arrows bore the words "my Lord commanded me" and "my Lord forbade me". Muhammad bin Ishaq and others say that the chief idol of Quraysh, Hubal, stood inside the Ka'bah, and that seven arrows were kept near it and drawn to settle disputes. Al-Bukhari recorded that when the Prophet ﷺ entered the Ka'bah after the conquest of Makkah, he saw pictures of Ibrahim and Isma'il holding the arrows, and he said: may Allah fight them, they never used the arrows for decisions. Mujahid described the arrows as the ones the Arabs used, and the dice the Persians and Romans used for gambling. The material notes this is doubtful unless the arrows were used both for gambling and for decisions at different times. It also notes that the same practice appears in 5:90 and 5:91, where the arrows are named together with intoxicants and gambling as an abomination of Shaytan's work. The verse says this practice is a serious departure from obedience and a form of associating partners with Allah. The believer seeks guidance from Allah instead, and the material cites the report of Jabir bin 'Abdullah, which Ahmad, al-Bukhari and the collectors of the Sunan recorded. The Prophet ﷺ taught his Companions the prayer of istikharah, a voluntary two rak'ahs and a prayer asking Allah to choose the good for them, in all their affairs, just as he taught them a surah of the Qur'an. The material notes that Ahmad and At-Tirmidhi, who graded it Hasan Sahih Gharib, record its wording.

**"This is all evil"** is the verse's summary. The material says that the word for it refers to disobedience, sin, misguidance, ignorance and, above all, the association of partners with Allah. Since drawing lots is a form of that association, the Qur'an calls the whole list an abomination. Ibn 'Abbas and others said that Allah wants the believers to seek the decision from Him, after first worshipping Him.

**"Today the disbelievers have given up all hope of ˹undermining˺ your faith"** speaks of a day. The material gives this as the day of 'Arafah in the tenth year after the Hijrah, when the Muslims stood at the Plain of 'Arafah with the Prophet ﷺ. The disbelievers had hoped to bring the believers back to their old religion, and by this point they had no hope of it. Ibn 'Abbas explained that they gave up hope that the Muslims would return to their religion. The material links this to a saying in the two Sahih collections, that Shaytan has despaired of being worshipped in the Arabian Peninsula, though he will still stir trouble among its people.

**"So do not fear them; fear Me!"** is the instruction to the believers, not to be afraid of the disbelievers, because they now have no power to harm them, but to fear Allah alone. The material says that the believers were to stand firm, be patient, oppose the disbelievers in what they do, and fear none but Allah, who would grant them victory, raise them above their enemies in this life and in the next, and please their hearts.

**"Today I have perfected your faith for you, completed My favour upon you, and chosen Islam as your way"** is the most discussed sentence in the passage. The material gives three rewards in it. The first is the perfection of the religion. Ibn 'Abbas explained that this means all the limits, obligations, rules and refinements of personal and social conduct have been completed, so that nothing needs to be added and nothing is missing. The material says that no new rule was revealed after this, apart from a few verses of encouragement and reminder. The jurists who work out new rulings by careful reasoning, called ijtihad, do not add anything to this perfection, because their rulings rest on principles that the Qur'an itself laid down. The second reward is the completion of the favour. The material explains this as the rise of the Muslims and the defeat of their enemies, shown in the conquest of Makkah, the end of the customs of ignorance, and the absence of disbelievers from the Hajj that year. The third reward is that Allah has chosen Islam as the religion of this community, the last and most complete religion, after which no other will come. The material notes a difference in the wording. "Perfection" is the purpose of the law being completed, and "completion" is that nothing more is needed. The religion is attributed to the believers, because it is shown in what they do, and the favour is attributed to Allah, because it comes from Him.

The material also says that the perfection does not mean the earlier prophets had an imperfect faith. Each prophet's religion was complete for its own time and people. Islam is different because it was sent last and is meant for every time, place and people until the Last Day. The material adds that this completion was the climax of a faith that began with Adam and continued through the prophets, and that this final form was given to the Last of the Prophets ﷺ and to his community.

Some reports describe the reaction of the Companions. A Jewish man said to 'Umar bin al-Khattab that if this verse had been revealed to them, they would have made the day of its revelation a festival. 'Umar replied that he knew exactly when and where it was revealed, on the evening of 'Arafah on a Friday. In another report, 'Umar wept when the verse came down, and the Prophet ﷺ asked why. 'Umar said the verse seemed to mean that the time of the Prophet ﷺ in this world was nearing its end, because the religion had now been perfected. The Prophet ﷺ agreed with him. The material notes that the Prophet ﷺ died eighty-one days after the revelation of the verse.

The material draws a lesson from 'Umar's answer. Islam does not make festivals of the births, deaths or anniversaries of people, and it does not turn historical events into celebrations as other peoples did. Instead, it marks acts of worship and principles. The two festivals of Islam are 'Id al-Fitr after Ramadan and 'Id al-Adha after the Hajj. The material notes that the Night of Deliverance, Laylat al-Bara'ah, the Night of Power, the Day of 'Arafah and the Day of 'Ashura are honoured because of the acts of worship linked to them. It criticises later invented celebrations, including the birthday of the Prophet ﷺ, as having no basis in the words or deeds of the Companions or the early righteous generations.

**"But whoever is compelled by extreme hunger—not intending to sin—then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"** is the exception. The material explains that a person who faces death from hunger may eat a little of what is forbidden, just enough to remove the danger, and not to satisfy appetite. His heart must not be inclined to sin. The verse is an exception to the general rule, and it does not make the forbidden things lawful in themselves. The material says that the phrase about forgiveness shows the prohibition still stands and that only the person in this state is granted leave. The reports add that the permission does not require a waiting period of three days, as some unlearned people believed. Ahmad recorded that Abu Waqid al-Laythi asked the Prophet ﷺ when they might eat carrion in a land where famine was common, and he said: when you find no food for your meal and no produce, then eat from it. The material says the chain of this report meets the standard of the two Sahih collections. The Prophet ﷺ also said, as recorded by Ibn Hibban and in the Musnad, that Allah likes His permissions to be taken, just as He dislikes to be disobeyed. A verse of Surat al-Baqarah gives the same exception with the condition that one neither wilfully disobeys nor goes beyond the necessary limit. The material notes that some scholars took this to mean a traveller who sets out to sin does not receive the concessions of travel.

### The fish and the locust

The reports make two exceptions to the rule of carrion. Ibn 'Umar, in a report collected by Ibn Majah, ad-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi and Ahmad through 'Abdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam, says the Prophet ﷺ allowed two dead things and two kinds of blood. The dead things are fish and locust. The bloods are the liver and the spleen. The material notes that 'Abdur-Rahman is a weak narrator. The material also records that Abu Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ, asked about the sea, said its water is pure and its dead are lawful, and this report was collected by Malik in the Muwatta, by Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah in their Sunan, and by Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn Hibban in their Sahih collections. The material notes that the same rule covers locusts, as a later report shows.

### Why the forbidden things are harmful

The material explains the reasons. Some animals are harmful to the body, because disease can pass from them, or to morals and character. These the Qur'an declares evil and unlawful. Carrion is unlawful partly because its blood stays in its flesh and is not drawn out, as it is when the animal is slaughtered properly. Blood is forbidden as it is poured out, and the slaughter of an animal properly is the way it is drained. The material adds that other forms of killing do not drain the blood in the same way. This is the reason for the careful method of slaughter, dhabh, which makes sure the blood flows out. The material also notes that many other things in the animal's body besides the flesh are unfit to eat.

Some scholars explained the prohibition of swine and of invoked animals as a matter of purity: both are associated with unbelief and with things that corrupt the soul. The material says that for this reason the meat of an animal slaughtered in the name of a false god is unlawful in itself, whatever the method of slaughter.

### The inner meaning

The material also gives a reading that uses the verse to describe the soul. It says that an animal's flesh has two conditions. When it is killed in the proper way under the law, it is clean and may be eaten. When it dies by itself, it is defiled. In the same way, when the human self is slain in the struggle for discipline, subdued by religion, made a servant of the law and humbled by the burden of obedience, the soul becomes clean and close. But when a soul dies in heedlessness, no longer aware of the religion and no longer working within the limits of the law, it becomes like carrion, which must be avoided. The same reading takes the Qur'anic phrase about the strangled, the beaten and the fallen as images of the states of the soul.

The material also cites a report, given by Ibn Hibban, that a Muslim's backbiting is a form of carrion worse than the rest. The Qur'an, in 49:12, forbids backbiting. The material says that the prohibition is stronger here, and that it is never allowed under compulsion or free choice.

### In short

- The verse forbids carrion, blood, swine, the animal slaughtered for a name other than Allah, and the animals killed by strangling, beating, a fall, a goring or a predator, unless they can be properly slaughtered.
- It forbids the animals sacrificed on stone altars and the use of arrows to decide matters, which the material calls an abomination and a form of associating partners with Allah.
- It names the day of 'Arafah in the tenth year as the time when the religion was perfected, the favour completed and Islam chosen as the way of the community.
- It allows a person in extreme hunger, without any intention to sin, to eat what is otherwise forbidden, only as much as needed to save him.
- The material also links the verse to lessons about festivals, the nature of the soul, and the prohibition of backbiting.

4.text:
This verse answers a question that the believers had asked the Prophet ﷺ. They asked what they were allowed to eat. The verse replies: "They ask you, ˹O Prophet,˺ what is permissible for them ˹to eat˺." The answer is that what is good and lawful is permitted, and so is what trained hunting animals and birds of prey catch for their owners, provided the owner mentions the Name of Allah when he sends them out. The believer is to eat that game, having first mentioned the Name of Allah over it. The verse ends with a reminder: "And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah is swift in reckoning." The two halves belong together. The verse first widens the permission, and then it places a condition on it, which is that the believer must remember Allah both at the beginning of the hunt and at the meal.

The verse follows the list of forbidden food in 5:3, and the phrase about what has been earned points back to 6:60, where Allah says He knows what you have earned by day. Having named what is forbidden, the Qur'an now names what is lawful, so that the believer knows both sides of the rule. The material says the question was about hunting with trained dogs and falcons, and this verse is the answer. A report in the material says the question was asked when Gabriel, who had been granted permission to enter, would not enter a house that had a picture or a dog in it, and a puppy was found there. Abu Rafi', who was sent to kill the dogs in Madinah, spared a woman's dog and was told to kill it, and then people asked what was lawful for them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They ask you, ˹O Prophet,˺ what is permissible for them ˹to eat˺."** The question was put to the Prophet ﷺ. The material names the people who asked as Zayd bin Muhalhil al-Ta'i and 'Adi bin Hatim al-Ta'i, both of whom were fishermen. Another report tells of a time when the Prophet ﷺ had ordered the killing of dogs in Madinah. People then asked what was lawful for them from a community whose dogs they had been ordered to kill. This report is given as the occasion for the verse.

**"Say, 'What is good and lawful.'"** The Prophet ﷺ is told to answer. The material explains the word at-tayyibat as "the good things". Muqatil said it covers everything Muslims are allowed and every kind of provision that is earned legally. Al-Qurtubi and the commentary tradition take it in the same way, as what is clean, sound and suitable. The material notes that in Surat al-A'raf the Prophet ﷺ is described as allowing good things and forbidding filthy things. Az-Zuhri was asked about drinking urine for medicine and said that this is not one of the good things. Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded this statement.

**"Also what is caught by your hunting animals and birds of prey which you have trained as instructed by Allah."** The Arabic word for these animals is jawarih, which comes from a root meaning to earn or to gain. The Arabs would say that someone earned something good for his family in this sense. The material says the word covers trained hunting dogs, falcons, wild cats and any beast or bird that can be trained to hunt. Ibn 'Abbas said this, and Khaythamah, Tawus, Mujahid, Makhul and Yahya bin Abi Kathir were reported to agree. The majority of the Companions, the next generation and the imams held that game caught by trained birds of prey is lawful in the same way as game caught by trained dogs, because birds of prey catch with their claws, just as dogs catch with their teeth. Ibn 'Umar, in a report of Ibn Jarir, held that a falcon's catch is lawful only if the hunter reaches it alive, and otherwise not. 'Adi bin Hatim asked the Prophet ﷺ about game caught by a falcon. He said: whatever the falcon catches for you, eat it.

The material gives a clear test for a trained animal. It must catch the game with its claws or teeth, not kill it by the force of a blow alone. The training is shown by the animal's habit of bringing the prey to its master and not eating it. Ibn Jarir and others hold that the animal must hold the prey until the owner arrives. The lawfulness of the game is then agreed among the scholars, even if the animal has killed it.

**"training them as hounds"** describes the training. The material explains that the animal must be sent after the game, and when it catches the game it holds it for its owner and does not take a bite for itself. The material lists four conditions. First, the dog or falcon must be taught and disciplined, so that when it is released it catches the game and brings it back, and does not eat it. A falcon must return when called, even while chasing. If the dog eats the prey, or the falcon does not return, the game is no longer the owner's and may not be eaten. Second, the animal must be released by the owner's choice, not left to chase game on its own. The word used for training, mukallibin, is from the verb meaning to set a dog against game, and the commentary tradition takes it as a sending out. Third, the animal must bring the game to its owner and not eat it, as the phrase "what they hold for you" shows. Fourth, the owner must say the name of Allah when he releases the animal. When these conditions are met, game that is dead when it reaches the hunter may be eaten without a second slaughter. If they are not met, the game must be slaughtered before it can be eaten. One scholar, Abu Hanifah, adds a fifth condition, which is that the animal must have wounded the prey. The material says the word jawarih hints at this, since the word also means animals that wound. The material adds that wild game caught and held in captivity is not lawful without slaughter.

The material cites the report of 'Adi bin Hatim in the two Sahih collections. He asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he could send his hunting dog with the name of Allah, and the Prophet ﷺ said that if the dog catches the game and it is still alive, he must slaughter it. If the game is dead, and the dog did not eat from it, the hunter may eat it, because the dog has completed its slaughter. If the dog eats from the game, the hunter must not eat it, because the Prophet ﷺ said he fears that the dog caught it for itself. In another report, the Prophet ﷺ said that if the dog catches with the sharp edge the game may be eaten, and if it is killed by the broad side it may not. The material also records that if another dog joins the hunt, and the hunter did not mention the name of Allah over that second dog, the game may not be eaten.

**"so eat of what they catch for you, but pronounce the Name of Allah over it"** is the central command. The material says it means: when you send the animal out, say "In the Name of Allah". Ibn 'Abbas said that if you forget, there is no harm. Abu Tha'labah, in the two Sahih collections, reported that the Prophet ﷺ told the hunter to mention Allah's Name when he sends his dog, and also when he shoots an arrow. The verse is also read as a command to say the Name of Allah when eating, and the material cites the report in the two Sahih collections in which the Prophet ﷺ taught his stepson 'Umar bin Abi Salamah to say the Name of Allah, to eat with his right hand, and to eat from the part of the dish nearest to him. 'A'ishah, in a report collected by al-Bukhari, said that some people recently converted from disbelief brought meat, and the believers did not know whether the Name of Allah had been mentioned over it. The Prophet ﷺ said: mention the Name of Allah over it and eat it.

**"And be mindful of Allah."** The verse returns to taqwā. The material explains that this means keeping the commands of Allah and staying away from what He forbids. The believer who hunts with a trained animal, or who eats its catch, is still under the law of Allah.

**"Surely Allah is swift in reckoning."** The verse ends with a warning that Allah reckons quickly. One reading explains that the phrase is a reminder that His punishment is severe for those who neglect what He has commanded.

### Why the trained animal is lawful

The material explains the reasoning. A trained hunting animal is lawful because it hunts on behalf of its master. It has learned to act according to human purpose, and so it stands in the place of its master. The material says that things that nature regards as clean and well formed, and animals whose nature fits the human nature, are lawful, provided no defect has appeared in them for reasons of health or of the law. The human mind cannot always apply this principle correctly, so the Qur'an gives the principle together with its right application.

### The hunt and the prayer

The material ends with a warning. Hunting with a trained animal is permitted, but it is not allowed to neglect the prayer and other duties for the sake of the pleasure of chasing game.

### In short

- The verse answers a question about what is lawful to eat, and it says that the good things are lawful.
- Game caught by trained dogs or birds of prey is lawful, provided the animal was trained, was released by its owner, did not eat the catch, and was sent out with the Name of Allah.
- The believer must say the Name of Allah when sending the animal and again when eating.
- The verse ends with a call to be mindful of Allah, because Allah reckons swiftly.

5.text:
This verse opens with a general permission and then gives two particular ones. The general one is: "Today all good, pure foods have been made lawful for you." The first particular one allows the food of the People of the Book, meaning their properly slaughtered animals, and allows them to eat what the believers slaughter. The second allows a believer to marry a chaste woman from among the believers, and also a chaste woman from among those who were given the Scripture before, on condition that he gives her dowry and keeps to marriage. It forbids a man to have a woman in secret or to keep her as a mistress. The verse ends with a warning: whoever rejects the faith, all his good deeds are void, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers. The verse therefore does three things: it opens the good foods, it makes lawful a marriage, and it reminds the reader that faith is the condition that makes any deed count.

The verse comes straight after the list of forbidden foods in 5:3 and the permission for trained hunting in 5:4. The material reads it as the completion of that discussion, and it says the word "today" refers to the day of 'Arafah in the tenth year after the Hijrah, the same day as the verse about the completion of the religion.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Today all good, pure foods have been made lawful for you"** begins with a general permission. The word translated as good and pure is at-tayyibat. The material explains that the word is set against al-khaba'ith, the foul and disgusting things, so that the verse states the principle that everything good and beneficial is lawful and everything foul and harmful is not. Muqatil said it covers everything Muslims are allowed and every legally earned provision. One reading argues that human beings are not like animals whose life is only eating and sleeping. Their purpose is higher, and that purpose requires high and pure morals. The material says that what enters the body becomes part of the person and so affects his conduct, which is why the lawful and the good matter so much. It gives unlawful income from theft, robbery, bribery, interest and gambling as examples of things that take a person away from humanity. The material also cites 23:51, which tells the messengers to eat of the good things and do righteous deeds, and it says the two commands are linked. Eating what is lawful is part of righteous conduct.

The material gives a further principle. Some things are judged good or evil by the sound taste of a person of good nature. Carrion and blood are judged disgusting by such people in every period. But where custom has blunted that taste, or where the evil is hidden, the decision of the prophets is the guide. The prophets, the material says, were protected and raised by Allah so that they could tell good from evil. Shah Waliyyullah is quoted as saying that the forbidden animals fall under two principles. One is an animal that is evil by its nature, and the other is an animal that was not slaughtered in the right way, so that it counts as carrion.

**"Similarly, the food of the People of the Book is permissible for you and yours is permissible for them."** This is the permission for the slaughtered animals of the People of the Book. The material says that a long line of early authorities read "food" here as animals properly slaughtered. Among them are Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and as-Suddi, together with several others. The reason given is that the People of the Book, like the believers, say the name of Allah over the animals and hold that slaughter for anyone else is forbidden. The material says the scholars agreed on this. Ibn Hatim and other reports say that 'Abdullah bin Mughaffal reported that during the siege of Khaybar someone threw a leather bag of fat, which the believers took as booty. The material says the fat was taken before the division of the booty, which the scholars use as evidence that a person may eat what he needs from the booty first. The Hanafi, Shafi'i and Hanbali scholars took it as evidence for eating parts of the Jewish slaughter that the Jews themselves avoid, such as the fat. The Maliki scholars disagreed. A stronger proof, the material says, is the report of the poisoned leg of sheep that the people of Khaybar offered the Prophet ﷺ. He took a bite, the animal told him it was poisoned, and he spat it out. Bishr bin al-Bara' bin Ma'rur died from eating it, and the Prophet ﷺ had the woman who poisoned it put to death. The material notes that the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions ate from that animal without asking the Jews whether the fat had been removed.

The material explains the second half of this phrase, "and yours is permissible for them", as permission for believers to give their own slaughtered meat to the People of the Book. The Prophet ﷺ gave his robe to 'Abdullah bin Ubayy bin Salul to wrap him when he died, because 'Abdullah had once given his own robe to al-Abbas. A report says do not befriend anyone but a believer, nor let anyone but a righteous person eat your food, and the material says it is meant to encourage such conduct.

The later scholars then take up the question of who counts as the People of the Book. The material says the term applies to those who hold a scripture that is certainly from Allah, such as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms of David, and to the followers of those scriptures. It does not apply to peoples who claim a book without proof, such as the idolaters of Makkah, the Magians, the Hindus, the Buddhists or others. The Sabians are described as unclear, and some scholars include them and others do not. The material says that the Jews and Christians are the People of the Book by universal agreement. Those who distorted their scriptures, and who took 'Uzayr or the Messiah as sons or partners of Allah [9:30], remain called the People of the Book, because the Qur'an keeps this name for them even while it describes their distortions [5:13]. The material gives the example of a governor who asked 'Umar about people who read the Torah and kept the Sabbath but did not believe in the Last Day. 'Umar replied that they should be treated as a sect of the People of the Book. The material then says that people who are listed as Jews or Christians in census records, but who do not believe in God or accept Musa or 'Isa as prophets, do not count under this rule.

Ibn al-Jawzi reports that 'Ali said not to eat from the animals slaughtered by Christians of Bani Taghlib, because they had taken nothing from Christianity except drinking wine. Al-Shafi'i is said to have transmitted this with sound authority. The majority of the Companions and Successors, however, found that these people were ordinary Christians who had never left their faith. So they ruled that their slaughter was lawful too. Al-Qurtubi says the majority of jurists hold that the slaughter of Christians is lawful, whatever tribe they belong to, and the same is true of every Jew. The material concludes that Christians who are known for certain not to believe in God or in Musa and 'Isa as prophets are not covered by the rule.

The material also explains what "food" means. Literally it means anything eaten. But most scholars hold that here it means meat slaughtered by the People of the Book, because dry foods like wheat, chickpeas, rice and fruit are open to all and need no slaughter. As for food that has been handled by non-Muslims, the careful practice is to avoid it where there is no need, because the purity of their utensils and hands cannot be relied on. Al-Qurtubi argues that food that needs an act of production, such as bread or pressed oil, may be refused out of simple distaste, but that slaughter is different because it requires faith and intention. Ordinarily a slaughter by an unbeliever would not be valid, but the Qur'an makes the slaughter of the People of the Book lawful as an exception, as Ibn 'Abbas explained.

**"And ˹permissible for you in marriage˺ are chaste believing women"** begins the marriage permission. The material says that this covers free, chaste believing women. It refers to women who do not commit fornication, which the word "chaste" makes clear. It is set against 2:221, which forbids marrying idolatresses until they believe, and against 4:25. The material reports that 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar advised against marrying Christian women, because he said the worst form of association with Allah is a woman's claim that 'Isa is her lord, and he quoted 2:221. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said that when 2:221 came down, the people stopped marrying pagan women. When this verse came, they married women from the People of the Book. Some Companions married Christian women and saw no problem in it, reading this verse as an exception to 2:221, while others held that 2:221 covered the People of the Book as well. The material says the two verses do not contradict, because the People of the Book were named separately when the other idolaters were named [98:1] and [3:20].

**"and chaste women of those given the Scripture before you"** gives the wider group of women. The material explains that a Jewish or Christian woman may be married on the same condition, that she is chaste.

**"as long as you pay them their dowries in wedlock, neither fornicating nor taking them as mistresses"** lays down the conditions. The dowry, mahr, must be paid with a good heart. The material notes the view of Jabir bin 'Abdullah, 'Amir ash-Sha'bi, Ibrahim an-Nakha'i and al-Hasan al-Basri that if a woman commits adultery before the marriage is consummated, the marriage is annulled and she returns the dowry. Men as well as women must be chaste, and a man must not take a woman as a secret lover, as the Qur'an forbids in 4:25 and as the material explains in its discussion of Surat an-Nisa'.

**"And whoever rejects the faith, all their good deeds will be void ˹in this life˺ and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers"** closes the verse. The material explains that without faith good deeds have no true value. A deed counts only when it is done for Allah, and a deed done for oneself does not. One reading says that the believer who fears God keeps the law in its true spirit, and that the law does not guard a person who has no inclination of his own. One reading takes "losers" to mean that the disbeliever is deprived of Paradise and enters the Fire. Another reads the voiding of deeds the same way, saying that the condition for good deeds to be accepted is true faith.

### Why a Muslim man may marry a woman of the People of the Book

The material gives a reason. Muslim women may not marry non-Muslim men, but Muslim men may marry women from the People of the Book on certain conditions. One reading says this is because a woman is more easily influenced. Once she enters married life, she may be drawn to the faith and the society of her Muslim husband, so the marriage may become the start of her entry into Islam. One scholar adds that the two communities share the same rules on forbidden degrees of marriage, on public marriage and on the presence of two witnesses, so the marriage is not a matter of breaking the law.

### What the slaughter requires

The material also explains why the name of Allah must be spoken over slaughter. The Qur'an makes it obligatory to say the name at slaughter, but it only recommends saying "Bismillah" when eating. The reasoning is that an animal's life is taken, so the act must be marked by gratitude to Allah, while grain and fruit grow for human use and do not need such a mark. The material also says that Islam replaced the pagan practice of naming idols at slaughter with the naming of Allah, which was a practical way to wean people from their old customs.

### The People of the Book and the idolaters

The material compares the slaughter of the People of the Book with the slaughter of idolaters. Idolaters do not claim any scripture or any prophet sent by Allah, so their slaughter is not lawful, while the People of the Book claim a scripture, and their rules on slaughter and marriage are still close to Islam's. The material records a view that the verse makes the food of the People of the Book lawful because their own religion still requires the name of Allah at slaughter, and it forbids slaughter for anyone else. The material says the verses on slaughter in the earlier surahs, al-Baqarah and al-An'am, remain in force, and that this verse is not an abrogation of them. Ibn Jarir and Abu Hayyan are reported to have held that there was no abrogation, and the majority of the Companions held the same view. The material says that some Successors allowed the slaughter of the common People of the Book even when they named Masih or 'Uzayr, and this was based on their knowledge that the wider community had not left its original faith.

The material records Ibn al-Arabi asking his teacher Abu al-Fath al-Maqdisi about Christians of his time who named Masih or 'Uzayr when they slaughtered. Al-Maqdisi replied that the rule that governs them is like that of their forefathers. Allah knew this condition, and He made them subordinate to their forefathers.

### In short

- The verse opens the good and pure foods and makes lawful the slaughter of the People of the Book, on the understanding that they still say the name of Allah and reject slaughter for others.
- A believing man may marry a chaste believing woman or a chaste woman of the People of the Book, on condition that he gives her dowry and keeps to marriage.
- The verse links lawful food and good conduct, and it says that faith is the condition under which any good deed has value.
- The material notes that the scholars differ over who counts as the People of the Book and over the slaughter of certain Christian groups, and it reports the view of the majority in each case.

6.text:
This verse sets out the washing that a believer performs before prayer. It names the washing of the face, the washing of the hands up to the elbows, the wiping of the head and the washing of the feet up to the ankles. It then sets out the full bath after major impurity, and the substitute of clean earth for a person who cannot find water because he is ill, travelling, has relieved himself, or has been intimate with his wife. It ends by saying that Allah does not want to put the believers in difficulty, but wants to purify them and to complete His favour upon them, so that they may give thanks. The material places the revelation of this verse in the story of a necklace of 'A'ishah that was lost on the road back to Madinah, after which the Prophet ﷺ stopped and there was no water at dawn. The verse is the first place in the chapter where the rules of worship are set down, after the earlier verses dealt with food and marriage.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! When you rise up for prayer, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, and wash your feet to the ankles."** The command is tied to the moment of standing for prayer. The material explains that wudu is obligatory when a person is in a state of impurity and recommended when he is already pure. It reports that early in Islam a believer had to perform wudu for every prayer, and that this was later eased. Sulayman bin Buraydah reported from his father that the Prophet ﷺ performed wudu before every prayer. On the day of the conquest of Makkah he performed it once, wiped over his leather socks, and prayed the five prayers with that one wudu. 'Umar asked him about the change, and the Prophet ﷺ replied that he had done it on purpose. Al-Fadl bin al-Mubashshir reported that he saw Jabir bin 'Abdullah pray several prayers with one wudu. Ubaydullah bin 'Abdullah bin 'Umar reported that Ibn 'Umar renewed his wudu for every prayer. The material cites a report from Asma' bint Zayd, through 'Abdullah bin Hanzalah, that the Prophet ﷺ was first commanded to renew his wudu for every prayer, and that when this became hard on him he was told to use the siwak for each prayer and to renew his wudu only when he became impure. The material concludes, as most scholars do, that renewing wudu for every prayer is encouraged and not obligatory.

The material gives several other sayings of the Prophet ﷺ on the same subject. When he came back from relieving himself and food was brought to him, he was asked whether he wanted to perform wudu, and he replied that he was not about to pray. He is also reported to have said that he was commanded to perform wudu when he stood up for prayer. These reports are recorded by Abu Dawud, At-Tirmidhi and Muslim.

**The intention and the Name of Allah.** The material argues that intention is required before wudu, because the verse says "when you stand to pray." It takes the phrase to mean "when you intend to pray," as in the idiom where someone is told to stand when the leader comes, meaning stand for him. It cites the saying recorded by Al-Bukhari and Muslim that actions are judged by their intentions, and that each person gets what he intended. It recommends saying the Name of Allah before wudu begins, and it cites the saying that there is no wudu for the person who does not mention the Name of Allah over it. It also recommends washing the hands three times before they are put into the water, especially after sleep, because one does not know where the hand has been during the night. Abu Hurayrah is reported to have said this in the Two Sahihs.

**The face and the beard.** The material says that the scholars of fiqh define the face as the area from the point where the hair on the head begins to the end of the chin, and from one ear to the other, whatever the amount of hair a person has. Abu Wa'il reported that he saw 'Uthman perform wudu and pass his fingers through his beard three times while washing his face, and that 'Uthman said he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do the same. At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah recorded this, and Al-Bukhari graded it as acceptable.
