**The arms to the elbows.** The material says that the word translated "up to" means that the elbows are included, and it cites a usage elsewhere in the Qur'an where the same word means "together with." It recommends washing a little of the upper arm beyond the elbow. The material records the saying that the Prophet's community will be called the people with radiant limbs on the Day of Rising because of the traces of wudu, and that whoever can increase the area of that radiance should do so. Muslim recorded a related report from Abu Hurayrah that the radiance of the believer reaches as far as the water of his wudu reaches.

**The head.** Here the material gives the fullest account of the wudu of the Prophet ﷺ. Malik bin 'Amr bin Yahya al-Mazini reported from his father that a man asked 'Abdullah bin Zayd bin 'Asim to show him how the Prophet ﷺ performed wudu. He asked for water, poured it over his hands and washed them twice, rinsed his mouth and nose three times, washed his face three times, washed his forearms to the elbows twice, and then passed his wet hands over his head from the front to the back and back to the front, ending at the nape of the neck. The material says these reports show that it is necessary to wipe the whole head. Abu Dawud recorded similar descriptions from Mu'awiyah and al-Miqdad bin Ma'dikarib. Humran bin Aban reported that he saw 'Uthman perform wudu in the same way, washing the hands three times, the face three times, the forearms three times, wiping the head, and then washing the feet three times. 'Uthman then said that the Prophet ﷺ had done the same and had said that whoever performs wudu like this and prays two units without thinking of anything else will have his past sins forgiven. Abu Dawud also recorded a version of 'Uthman's report in which the head was wiped once.

**The feet.** The verse orders washing the feet up to the ankles. The material reports that Ibn 'Abbas said the verse means washing, and that A long list of early authorities held the same position, among them Ibn Mas'ud, 'Urwah and Mujahid, and the material names several more. The material says this clearly shows that the feet must be washed, and that wiping over the top of the bare foot is not enough. It cites reports from 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Mu'awiyah and al-Miqdad, showing the Prophet ﷺ washing his feet once, twice or three times. In a report recorded in the Two Sahihs, 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said that during a journey the Prophet ﷺ caught up with a group who were hurrying their wudu and only wiping their feet, and he called out in a loud voice that they should perform wudu thoroughly and save their heels from the Fire. Abu Hurayrah and 'A'ishah are reported to have said the same. 'Abdullah bin al-Harith bin Jaz' reported that the Prophet ﷺ said to save the heels and the soles from the Fire. Al-Bayhaqi and Al-Hakim recorded this with a sound chain. Muslim recorded that Umar bin al-Khattab saw a man leave a dry spot the size of a fingernail on his foot, and that the Prophet ﷺ told him to go back and perform wudu properly. Anas bin Malik reported a similar case. Ahmad recorded that some of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ reported a man praying with a dry spot the size of a dirham on his foot, and that he was told to repeat his wudu and his prayer. Abu Dawud collected this report from Baqiyyah, and the material says its chain is strong and reasonably good.

**The fingers.** Humran's report says that 'Uthman washed between his fingers. The collectors of the Sunan recorded Laqit bin Sabrah's question about wudu. The Prophet ﷺ replied that wudu should be performed thoroughly, that the fingers should be washed between each other, and that the nose should be rinsed well unless the person is fasting.

**The socks.** The material records that wiping over the leather socks is an established part of the Sunnah. Ahmad and Abu Dawud recorded Aws bin Abi Aws, who saw the Prophet ﷺ perform wudu, wipe over his socks, and then stand for prayer. Ahmad also recorded Jarir bin 'Abdullah al-Bajali, who embraced Islam after this chapter was revealed and then saw the Prophet ﷺ wipe over his socks. Hammam reported that Jarir wiped over his socks after relieving himself and said that he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do the same. Al-A'mash reported that Ibrahim said the scholars liked this report because Jarir embraced Islam after the chapter was revealed. The material says the practice reaches the level of widely transmitted reports, and that the Prophet ﷺ is described by both word and deed as wiping over his socks.

**"And if you are in a state of ˹full˺ impurity, then take a full bath."** The full bath is required after major impurity. The material says the rule is clear and needs little explanation. It is the same rule that is set out in the verse of the chapter on women, and the material points the reader there.

**"But if you are ill, on a journey, or have relieved yourselves, or have been intimate with your wives and cannot find water, then purify yourselves with clean earth by wiping your faces and hands."** The material says that the permission covers four cases: illness, travel, the call of nature, and sexual relations, and that a person who cannot find water after searching for it may use clean earth. The material says the earth is struck once with the hands and the face and hands are wiped with it. The material says the earth must be clean, as the Qur'an says, and it notes that the striking is to be done with two blows according to some readings, one for the face and one for the hands. The Prophet ﷺ is described as confirming that the whole of the two parts must be covered. It adds that the verse was revealed in connection with 'A'ishah's necklace. On the road back to Madinah the necklace was lost at the place called al-Bayda. The Prophet ﷺ stopped there and slept with his head in her lap. Abu Bakr came and struck her in the side and said she had delayed the people for a necklace. She wished she could not move, because the Prophet ﷺ was asleep and because of the pain. The Prophet ﷺ woke at dawn, there was no water, and the verse came down. Usayd bin al-Hudayr said to Abu Bakr's family that Allah had made the people blessed through them. The material records this as part of the story. Ibn Jarir and others also recorded it.

**"It is not Allah's Will to burden you, but to purify you and complete His favour upon you, so perhaps you will be grateful."** The material says that Allah made the rules easy for the believers, and that dry ablution is a mercy for the sick and for those without water. It explains that dry ablution is a substitute for wudu and is valid for the same things as wudu, except for certain matters. The purpose is purity, and the favour is the easy and gentle law. The verse ends by asking for gratitude, which the material says is the right response to the ease of the law.

### The virtue of wudu and what follows it

The material says that the Sunnah encourages a supplication after wudu, and that the person who does so is among those who seek purity, as the verse says. 'Uqbah bin 'Amir reported that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say that any Muslim who performs wudu well, and then prays two units with his heart and face turned to Allah, will enter Paradise. 'Umar was nearby and added that when a person completes wudu and says the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, the eight gates of Paradise open for him, so that he may enter by whichever he wishes. Abu Hurayrah reported in Malik's collection that when a believer washes his face, every sin his eyes committed leaves his face with the water, and the same is true of his hands and his feet, until he is free of sin. Abu Malik al-Ash'ari reported that the Prophet ﷺ said purity is half of faith, that the praise of Allah fills the scale, that fasting is a shield, that patience is a light, that charity is evidence of faith, and that the Qur'an is proof for or against a person. Ibn 'Umar reported that Allah does not accept charity from someone who has taken what is not his, or prayer without purity. The material says these reports link wudu to the whole of the believer's conduct.

### In short

- The verse sets out wudu in order, with the full bath after major impurity and the dry substitute of clean earth for illness, travel, the call of nature and sexual relations.
- The verse presents these rules as a mercy and as a completion of Allah's favour, so that the believer may give thanks.
- The reports on wudu are many and well known, and they show that the feet must be washed, that the whole head must be wiped, and that wiping over socks is part of the Sunnah.

7.text:
"Remember Allah’s favour upon you and the covenant He made with you when you said, “We hear and obey.” And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart"

This verse turns from the rules of worship to the covenant that the believers made with Allah. It reminds them of the favour of guidance to Islam and of the pledge they gave to hear and obey, and it ends by calling them to taqwa, since Allah knows what the hearts hide. The material places the pledge in the time of allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ, and it links the verse to the call to justice in the verses that follow.

### Phrase by phrase

#### The favour and the pledge

**"Remember Allah's favour upon you and the covenant He made with you when you said, “We hear and obey.”"** The favour is the guidance to Islam. The covenant is the pledge that the believers gave when they accepted Islam, to hear and obey the Prophet ﷺ in ease and in difficulty, and not to dispute leadership with those who hold it by right. The material says this is the pledge the Companions gave when they embraced Islam, and it says the pledge bound them to accept the law they had taken on. The material cites 57:8, which asks what is wrong with the believers that they do not believe in Allah, when the Messenger calls them to believe in their Lord and has taken their covenant. Another reading takes the verse as a reminder to the Jews of the covenant they made to follow the Prophet ﷺ and to keep his law.

#### Taqwa

**"And be mindful of Allah."** The material says taqwa means being mindful of Allah in every time and situation, and it explains that it means keeping the commands and avoiding the prohibitions. It makes the point that the pledge is only kept by a person who fears Allah, because the law by itself does not guard the one who has no fear.

#### The knowledge of the heart

**"Surely Allah knows best what is hidden in the heart."** The verse closes by stating that Allah knows the secrets and thoughts that the hearts conceal. The material says this makes obedience a matter of the heart as well as the limbs, and that nothing is hidden from Allah. It links the verse to the next, which calls the believers to justice even when they have grievances against others.

### In short

- The believers are reminded of the favour of Islam and of the pledge they gave to hear and obey.
- The verse calls for taqwa in every situation, and it reminds the reader that Allah knows the secrets of the heart.

8.text:
"O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony. Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice. Be just! That is closer to righteousness. And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do"

This verse sets a rule of justice that holds even towards an enemy. The material says it repeats in substance a command given in the chapter of women, but in a different order and for a different reason. The verse says that hatred of a people must not push a believer into injustice. It asks him to stand firm for Allah as a witness who bears true testimony, to be just, and to be mindful of Allah, who knows what he does.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony."** The material says the phrase "stand firm for Allah" means standing for the truth for the sake of Allah, not for people or for reputation. The earlier verse in the chapter of women, 4:135, has the same command with the words in a different order, asking believers to stand for justice as witnesses for Allah. The material explains that putting "for Allah" first here closes the door on personal feeling. Abu Hayyan gives a delicate reason for the change of order between the two verses, and the material follows it. The Holy Qur'an uses the same testimony language in more than one place, and the word shahadah in the material is wider than testimony in a court. A person who stands for Allah will stand for justice, and the one who stands for justice will stand for none but Allah. In 4:135, where the concern is self, parents and kin, justice is put first so that no kinship can pass for service to Allah.

**"Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice."** The material explains that there are two main causes that keep people from justice. One is taking the side of oneself, friends or relatives, which 4:135 addresses. The other is enmity against someone, which this verse addresses. The material cites the account of the Companions in the Two Sahihs, through An-Nu'man bin Bashir, in which his father gave him a gift and his mother refused to accept it unless the Prophet ﷺ were made a witness. The Prophet ﷺ asked whether he had given the same to all his children. When he said no, the Prophet ﷺ told him to fear Allah and treat his children equally, and said he would not witness an injustice. The father then took back the gift. The material says this is the same principle at a smaller scale: a believer must not let his feelings change his fairness.

**"Be just! That is closer to righteousness."** The material notes that the word "closer" is read by some as meaning that justice is in fact the right course and not merely a nearer one. It says that no other course is open to a believer, so "closer" amounts to "is" in its effect. The material also records that some of the female Companions told 'Umar he was harsher than the Prophet ﷺ, and it notes that they meant the manner of his reproof and not the Prophet's conduct.

**"And be mindful of Allah."** The material says that taqwa means keeping the commands and avoiding the prohibitions in all matters, including justice and injustice.

**"Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do."** The verse closes by reminding the believer that Allah sees every act, and that He will repay him for it.

### Justice and the duty of testimony

The material links this verse to the duty of giving evidence. It cites 2:283, which says that concealing testimony is a grave sin, and 2:282, which says that neither the scribe nor the witness should be made to suffer. The material says that bearing testimony is wajib, an obligation, and that the verses in Surat al-Baqarah make concealing it a grave sin. It then argues that in modern courts, repeated summonses and long delays can make the witness a victim, and that a simpler procedure would restore the duty to testify without harm. The material widens the idea of testimony beyond the court. A medical certificate, a mark on an examination paper, a certificate of qualification and a vote are all forms of testimony, and a false one is a grave sin.

### The vote as testimony, recommendation and agency

In the sunnah and in the Holy Qur'an the word shahadah has a broad sense, and the material applies that sense to the vote. The material gives the vote three meanings. It is testimony that the candidate is worthy. It is also a recommendation, for which 4:85 says that whoever makes a good recommendation shares in its reward and whoever makes a bad one shares in its burden. And it is an agency, because the voter appoints a representative in matters that belong to the whole nation. The material concludes that a vote for an unworthy candidate is false testimony, an unjust recommendation and an improper agency all at once. It says that every Muslim, man and woman, must investigate a candidate before voting.

### In short

- The verse asks the believer to stand firm for Allah, to bear true testimony, and to be just even towards those he dislikes.
- Enmity must never push a believer into injustice, and taqwa must guide every judgment.
- The material links the verse to the duty of honest testimony in court and in daily life, including the vote.

9.text:
"Allah has promised those who believe and do good ˹His˺ forgiveness and a great reward"

The verse gives a promise to the believers who do good deeds. It gives two rewards, forgiveness and a great reward, and the material says the great reward is Paradise. It follows directly from the call to justice in 5:8, so that the promise is given to those who carry out that justice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah has promised those who believe and do good."** The promise is given to those who believe and who act on that belief by doing good. The material says that faith and good deeds are linked, so the promise does not go to belief alone or to deeds alone. It notes that the believer's good deeds are part of the means by which Allah's mercy reaches him.

**"His forgiveness and a great reward."** The material explains that the forgiveness is pardon for sins, and that the reward is Paradise. It adds that the believer is not admitted to Paradise purely on account of his deeds, but on account of Allah's mercy and favour. The deeds are the path that Allah has set for that mercy, so the believer should thank Allah for the whole of it.

### Mercy and deeds

The material says that a verse of promise is a comfort to the believer. No one can claim that his deeds alone have earned him Paradise, because even the one who does good remains in need of Allah's pardon. The verse therefore presents the work and the mercy together, so that the believer neither despairs of Allah's forgiveness nor relies on his own action alone. The material links this to the wider teaching that the path of righteousness has to be walked with humility.

### The reward and the path

The reward is described as great, and the material says that its greatness is part of Allah's generosity. It says that the believer is given the promise so that he will continue in good work, and that the forgiveness is what allows him to stand before Allah without fear. The verse thus gives the believer hope and a clear direction at the same time.

### In short

- The promise is given to those who believe and do good, and it includes forgiveness and a great reward.
- Deeds are the path to that reward, but the reward itself comes from Allah's mercy and favour.

10.text:
"As for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the residents of the Hellfire"

The verse is the counterpart of the promise in 5:9. It names those who reject faith and deny the signs of Allah, and it says that they are the people of the Fire. The material reads the two verses together, so that the choice between them is plain.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs."** The "signs" are the proofs and revelations of Allah. The material says that in the world Allah makes His presence known through signs in the form of arguments that cannot be refuted. A person who hears a clear argument and answers it with empty wordplay instead of accepting it is denying the signs, even if he never uses the word. The verse is aimed at the one who rejects the truth after it has been made clear.

**"They are the residents of the Hellfire."** The verse ends with the fate of those who deny the signs. The material says the Fire is the place where they are held, and it says that the verse warns those who hear the truth and refuse it.

### Two paths

The material reads 5:9 and 5:10 together. One group believes and does good, and receives forgiveness and a great reward. The other denies and receives the Fire. The material says that the arrangement of the two verses makes the choice clear. It also says that the signs of Allah are open to the reasoning mind, so the one who denies them cannot claim that he had no means of knowing. The material notes that the signs include both the arguments of the Qur'an and the evidence in the world around the person.

### Denial after clarity

The material says that the denial is the decisive point. A person who has not heard the truth is not in the same position as one who has heard it and turned away. The verse does not speak of ignorance but of denial after the signs have come, and that is why the warning is so direct.

### In short

- Those who deny Allah's signs, after the truth has been shown to them, are the people of the Fire.
- The verse is a warning, and it stands in contrast to the promise in the verse before it.

11.text:
"O believers! Remember Allah’s favour upon you: when a people sought to harm you, but He held their hands back from you. Be mindful of Allah. And in Allah let the believers put their trust"

The verse calls the believers to remember a favour from Allah. It recalls a time when a people wanted to harm them, and Allah held back their hands. It ends by calling the believers to be mindful of Allah and to put their trust in Him. The verse follows 5:7, where the covenant of hearing and obeying is recalled, so that the favour of protection is placed alongside the covenant.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Remember Allah’s favour upon you."** The material says the favour is protection from harm. It explains that the verse asks the believer to recollect Allah's protection with his heart and tongue, as an act of gratitude.

**"When a people sought to harm you, but He held their hands back from you."** The material records several reports of this protection. One account, given by Jabir, tells of a man from the tribe of Muharib named Ghawrath bin al-Harith. He told his people that he would kill the Prophet ﷺ. He came to him and found him sitting with his sword in his lap. He asked to see the sword, took it, and raised it to strike. Each time, Allah stopped him. The man asked whether the Prophet ﷺ was not afraid of him, and the Prophet ﷺ replied that Allah would protect him. The man returned the sword, and this verse came down. In another report, Jabir describes the Prophet ﷺ resting under a tree after a journey, with his sword hung on a branch. A Bedouin took the sword and asked who would save him now. The Prophet ﷺ answered "Allah," and the man repeated the question two or three times, and each time the answer was the same. The man then returned the sword without harm. Abdur-Razzaq reported this through Ma'mar and al-Zuhri, and the material notes that Ma'mar said Qatadah used to mention that some Arabs had sent this man to kill the Prophet ﷺ.

The material also gives a second setting. Muhammad bin Ishaq, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah are reported to have said the verse was revealed about the Banu an-Nadir, who plotted to drop a stone on the Prophet ﷺ when he came to them for help with a blood payment. Allah told him of the plot, and he returned to Madinah. The Banu an-Nadir were then expelled after a siege. Another reading takes the verse as referring to a plot by a people who wanted to kill the believers. The material says the reports differ, and it presents them side by side without choosing among them.

**"Be mindful of Allah."** The material says the believer must not think his protection is a reason to relax. He must remain mindful of Allah in keeping His instructions and avoiding His prohibitions.

**"And in Allah let the believers put their trust."** The material explains that trust in Allah is what the believer relies on when he is threatened. It says that Allah suffices those who trust Him and protects them from the plots of others.

### Favour and the covenant

The material links the verse to 5:7, where the believers are reminded of the covenant of hearing and obeying. It also cites 57:8, which asks the believers why they do not believe when the Messenger calls them to their Lord and has taken their covenant. The material says that remembering Allah's favour leads to gratitude, and that gratitude leads to obedience. The protection the verse describes is therefore a reason for the believers to keep the covenant they made.

### Protection and trust

The material says that the believer who has been protected must still act. Trust in Allah does not mean doing nothing. It means taking the right means and then relying on Allah for the result. The protection in the verse is a sign that Allah is able to hold back those who plot against His servants, and the believer's trust is the response to that certainty.

### In short

- The verse reminds the believers of Allah's protection from people who wanted to harm them.
- The reports of this protection are many and they differ on the occasion, but they agree that Allah held back the hands that were raised against the believers.
- The believer responds to this favour with taqwa and trust in Allah.

12.text:
"Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them and ˹then˺ said, “I am truly with you. If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax, believe in My messengers, support them, and lend to Allah a good loan, I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow. And whoever among you disbelieves afterwards has truly strayed from the Right Way.”"

This verse recalls a covenant that Allah made with the Children of Israel. He appointed twelve leaders from among them, one for each tribe, and He gave them a set of duties and a promise. The duties are prayer, alms-tax, belief in His messengers, support for them, and a good loan to Allah. The promise is forgiveness of sins and admission to Gardens with rivers. The verse closes with a warning that whoever disbelieves after this has strayed from the right way. The material places the verse within the chapter's wider reminder of the covenants that the believers and earlier communities made with Allah. It follows directly from 5:11, where the believers were reminded of Allah's protection, and it is linked to the earlier call to keep the covenant of hearing and obeying in 5:7.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them."** The material explains that the twelve were representatives of their tribes, each of whom took responsibility for his people keeping the covenant. The material reports that Muhammad bin Ishaq and Ibn 'Abbas said this happened when Musa was about to fight a powerful enemy in the land, and Allah commanded him to choose one leader from each tribe. The leaders bound their tribes as well as themselves, so the covenant was a shared responsibility. Some readings say the twelve were chieftains and others say they were messengers, and the material does not settle the point, so the entry records only what is agreed.

The material draws a parallel with the Muslims. When the Ansar of Madinah came to pledge at the 'Aqabah, twelve of their leaders gave the pledge on behalf of their people. Three were from the tribe of Aws, among them Usayd bin al-Hudayr, and nine were from Khazraj, among them Abu Umamah As'ad bin Zurarah, Sa'd bin ar-Rabi', 'Abdullah bin Rawahah, al-Bara' bin Ma'rur, 'Ubadah bin as-Samit, and al-Mundhir bin 'Amr. Ka'b bin Malik named them in a poem that Ibn Ishaq recorded. The material says this shows that a representative from each group was a sound method of binding a people to a pledge, because a man of the tribe knows its feelings better than an outsider.

The material also notes Islam's principle on lineage. It says that in Islam a person is honoured by his faith, not by his family, and it cites the Prophet's address at his last Hajj, which said that no one has priority over another on the basis of colour, language or lineage. The material does not say that family and tribe have no value in administration, only that they must not outweigh faith.

**"I am truly with you."** The material explains that Allah's words "I am with you" mean two things. The first is that Allah gives support, protection and help to those who keep the covenant. The second is that Allah knows everything they do, and no one can escape His knowledge by breaking the pledge. The phrase is therefore both an encouragement and a warning.

**"If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax."** The material says that the duties of prayer and zakat were enjoined on the Children of Israel before Islam, and that these are not peculiar to any one community. It states that other verses and reports show every prophet and every law enjoined them. The material notes that zakat is an obligation on each individual, and it observes that many people pay it grudgingly and in less than the full amount.

**"Believe in My messengers, support them."** The material explains that belief in the messengers comes before the duties of prayer and zakat in the order of faith, but in this covenant the duties are mentioned first. The reason it gives is that the messengers who were to come later were not yet present when the covenant was made. The material says that supporting the messengers means helping them to carry their message.

**"And lend to Allah a good loan."** The material explains that a good loan means spending with sincerity, without any worldly motive, and from what a person holds dear, not from what is left over or worthless. Spending for Allah is called a loan because the return of a loan is owed in law, custom and morality. The material explains that because zakat has been mentioned separately, the good loan refers to voluntary charity. It also gives an example of such charity: building a mosque, or supporting religious education when the state does not. The material notes that zakat is an individual obligation, while such communal duties are a collective obligation that is discharged when enough people take them up.

**"I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow."** The material says that the promised forgiveness covers sins and errors, and that the Gardens are the protection from what is feared and the attainment of what is sought.

**"And whoever among you disbelieves afterwards has truly strayed from the Right Way."** The material explains that the warning is for those who break the covenant after accepting it. They have not simply erred, but have left the straight path to their own harm. The material notes that a person who denies a covenant he has made is more blameworthy than one who never made it.

### The twelve springs and the twelve rulers

The number twelve recurs in the story. The material cites Allah's favour in Surat al-A'raf, 7:160, where He divided the people into twelve tribes, and where twelve springs gushed from the rock when Musa struck it with his staff. The material says that the number is unusual and that it has given rise to popular interpretations, and it treats the springs as a sign of the care Allah took to give each tribe its own share.

The material also reports the saying recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim, through Jabir bin Samurah, that the affairs of the people will remain in order while twelve leaders govern them. It records Abd al-Razzaq's view that these need not rule one after another without a break. On that reading, the four rightful caliphs, Abu Bakr, 'Umar al-Faruq, 'Uthman al-Ghani and 'Ali al-Murtada, are counted among them, and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz is accepted as the fifth.

### Those named as leaders at 'Aqabah

The material names the men who gave the pledge at 'Aqabah with more care. Rafi' bin Malik bin al-'Ajlan is named in the list from Khazraj, and 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram is also named there. Abu al-Haytham bin at-Tayhan is named from Aws, as one of the three. The material says the naming of these men was recorded in a poem by Ka'b bin Malik, and that the men acted by the Prophet's command, pledging obedience on behalf of their people.

### The covenant and the will to keep it

The material links the verse to the call in 5:8 to stand for justice and to be mindful of Allah, and to the call in 5:11 to recall the favour of Allah. Qatadah is reported to have said that a later verse, the one commanding the believers to fight those who do not believe in Allah, is linked to the pardon of this verse. The material links the verse to the call in 5:7 to be mindful of Allah. It says that the only thing that holds a person to a pledge is taqwa, the fear of Allah, and that where taqwa is absent, pledges are easily broken. It also says that the victory of the believers comes from taqwa and trust in Allah, not from weapons and wealth alone. The verse therefore closes by inviting the reader to reflect on the difference between the one who keeps the covenant and the one who breaks it.

### In short

- Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel through twelve representatives, and the covenant bound each tribe.
- The duties were prayer, zakat, belief and support for the messengers, and a good loan to Allah, with forgiveness and Paradise as the promise.
- Breaking the covenant after accepting it is straying from the right way, and only taqwa keeps a pledge in force.

13.text:
"But for breaking their covenant We condemned them and hardened their hearts. They distorted the words of the Scripture and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold. You ˹O Prophet˺ will always find deceit on their part, except for a few. But pardon them and bear with them. Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers"

This verse describes what followed the breaking of the covenant. Because they broke it, Allah removed them from His mercy and hardened their hearts. They altered the words of the Scripture from their places and forgot a portion of what they had been reminded of. The Prophet ﷺ is told that he will always find deceit among them, except for a few, and he is told to pardon them and bear with them, because Allah loves those who do good. The material explains the verse as a description of a community that has been punished for its wrongdoing, and as an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ to forgive them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But for breaking their covenant We condemned them and hardened their hearts."** The material explains that the curse is removal from Allah's mercy. The hardening of the hearts means that the people cannot accept advice or the truth. The material cites a reading that the hearts were made rusty and unable to accept good, which it links to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ that each sin leaves a dark mark on the heart. If a person repents, the mark is erased, but if he persists, the marks accumulate until his heart becomes like an upturned pot, which takes in nothing. The material says this is the cash punishment for sin in this world: one sin draws the heart to the next, and one good deed draws the heart to the next good deed.

**"They distorted the words of the Scripture."** The material says this includes changing the words of the Scripture, altering their meaning and changing their recitation. It says that these changes are described in the Qur'an and in the books of hadith. The material gives examples of their deceit against the believers, and it says that a plot was made to kill the Prophet ﷺ, which Allah revealed to him.

**"And neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold."** The material explains that they set aside part of their law, and that the portion they neglected concerned the description of the Prophet ﷺ and the duty to follow him.

**"You will always find deceit on their part, except for a few."** The material says that the exception refers to those who believed and held to the covenant. It gives the example of 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his followers. It also notes that the verse was read as a description of the Banu Qurayzah in one account.

**"But pardon them and bear with them."** The material explains that the Prophet ﷺ is told not to treat them with contempt, because after knowing their state, good advice is unlikely to reach them. Yet gentleness and forbearance can sometimes bring a person to his senses. The material cites the view of some early scholars that a gentle approach is better than revenge. It also says that a person's own conduct must remain correct, because the effort to set others right begins with oneself. This verse was, in the material's account, read as abrogated by the verse of the sword in Surat at-Tawbah, though other readings hold that the pardon remains in force.

**"Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers."** Mujahid is reported to have said the deceit refers to the plot against the life of the Messenger ﷺ, and the material says the surah al-Mutaffifin describes the stain that sin leaves on the heart. The material says that Allah loves those who act with good grace, and that this is the path that brings the believers nearer to Him. The material also says that the Torah contains the description of the Prophet ﷺ, which the people were bound to follow.

### The warning and the example

The material says that the verse serves as a warning against the same breaches that were committed by the earlier community. The believers are asked to keep their own covenant and to be patient with those who err. It notes that the believers must not repeat the behaviour that cost the earlier community the mercy of Allah.

### In short

- The Children of Israel were cursed and hardened for breaking their covenant, and they altered and neglected parts of the Scripture.
- The Prophet ﷺ is told to pardon them, because forbearance can sometimes reach a hard heart, and because Allah loves those who do good.
- The verse warns the believers to keep their own covenant and to avoid the path of the earlier people.

14.text:
"And from those who say, “We are Christians,” We took their covenant, but they neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold. So We let hostility and enmity arise between them until the Day of Judgment, and soon Allah will inform them of all they have done"

This verse turns to the Christians. It says that Allah took a covenant from those who called themselves Christians, but that they neglected part of what they were commanded. As a result, Allah stirred up enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Judgment. The verse ends by saying that Allah will tell them of all that they did. The material reads the verse as the parallel of the earlier case of the Children of Israel, with the division among the Christians as the punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And from those who say, “We are Christians,” We took their covenant."** The material explains that the covenant was in the Gospel, that they would follow the Prophet ﷺ, help him, honour him and believe in every prophet that Allah sends. The material says the Christians imitated the Jews in breaking their covenant.

**"But they neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold."** The material says that they set aside part of what they had been reminded of in the Gospel concerning faith and other matters.

**"So We let hostility and enmity arise between them until the Day of Judgment."** Al-Baydawi, in a marginal note on the verse, reports three early Christian groups: the Nestorians, who took 'Isa as the son of God, the Jacobites, who held that 'Isa was one with God, and the Melkites, who held that 'Isa was one of the Trinity. The material notes that such differences of belief made hostility inevitable. The verse 5:11 before this one recalls the same protection of the believers, so the verse 5:14 reads as the counterpart of the favour in 5:11. The material explains that the enmity is the division among Christian groups, who accused one another of heresy and disbelief. It names the groups that the material describes, and it says that these sects still disagree and refuse to pray in one another's places of worship. The material notes that the differences over the nature of 'Isa were the basis of the division. It also says that where the groups have no religious disagreement, the conflict does not arise, because the enmity was based on religion. One reading says the verse describes genuine Christians who practise the faith, and not those who have left it.

**"And soon Allah will inform them of all they have done."** The material says this is a warning and a threat to the Christians for their lies against Allah and His messenger, and for attributing a companion and a son to Allah. The material affirms that Allah is one and that He neither begets nor is begotten.

### The two communities

The material reads 5:13 and 5:14 together. The Jews and the Christians both received a covenant, both broke parts of it, and both were punished. In the Jews' case the punishment was a hardening of the heart and a loss of guidance, and in the Christians' case it was division and enmity among themselves. The material says that the verse 5:11 gives the believers the favour of protection, which the earlier people lost through breaking the covenant. The material says the verses show that breaking a covenant leads to the loss of unity and of guidance, whichever community is involved.

### In short

- Allah took a covenant from those who call themselves Christians, and they neglected part of it.
- Allah stirred up enmity among them until the Day of Judgment, and they will be told of their deeds.
- The verse shows that breaking a covenant brings division, as it did for the Jews, and it is a warning to the believers.

15.text:
"O People of the Book! Now Our Messenger has come to you, revealing much of what you have hidden of the Scriptures and disregarding much. There certainly has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book"

This verse addresses the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. It says that the Messenger has come to them, and that he makes plain much of what they had hidden from their Scriptures and passes over much of it. It then says that a light and a clear Book have come to them from Allah. The material explains that the Prophet ﷺ made clear the parts of their Scripture that they had altered or concealed, and left aside what would bring no benefit if it were explained. The verse presents the Qur'an as the clear light that replaces the darkness into which their own distortions had led them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O People of the Book! Now Our Messenger has come to you."** The material explains that the address is to the Jews, who had the Torah, and to the Christians, who had the Gospel. The word "now" marks the arrival of the Messenger after the earlier revelations.

**"Revealing much of what you have hidden of the Scriptures and disregarding much."** The material says that the Prophet ﷺ explained the places where they had changed, distorted and lied about Allah, and that he ignored much of what they had altered, since explaining it would bring no benefit. Al-Hakim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said that whoever denies stoning as the punishment for adultery has denied the Qur'an, because stoning was among the things the People of the Book had hidden, and this verse revealed it. The material adds that Al-Hakim said the chain of this report was sound.

**"There certainly has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book."** The light is the Prophet ﷺ, and the clear Book is the Qur'an. The material explains that the Qur'an is light and plain guidance, and it contrasts the Qur'an with the darkness of distortion.

### The truth made clear

The material says that the Messenger came with the guidance and the religion of truth for all people, Arabs and non-Arabs, those who could read and those who could not. He came with clear proofs and a clear distinction between truth and falsehood. The verse therefore ends the concealment that had hidden the truth from people, and it shows the purpose of the Messenger's mission as making the truth plain.

One reading in the material says that the People of the Book had made two mistakes. They omitted parts of their teaching, or distorted it, so that they did not need a new prophet. They also imposed restrictions that Allah had not commanded, through the subtle reasoning of their scholars. The Qur'an, the material says, restored their teaching to its original form and freed them from the burdens they had added. The material adds that the truth is shown by argument, and that reason appeals to those whose minds are open. The false deities that people set up cannot create or destroy anything, and that alone shows that there is no god but the one God.

### In short

- The Messenger came to the People of the Book and made clear the parts of their Scriptures that they had hidden or altered.
- The Qur'an is a light and a clear Book from Allah, which restores the truth they had lost.
- The verse shows that the purpose of the Messenger's mission is to make the truth plain to all.

16.text:
"through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace, brings them out of darkness and into light by His Will, and guides them to the Straight Path"

This verse says what the clear Book does. It guides those who seek the pleasure of Allah to the ways of peace, brings them out of darkness and into light by His will, and leads them to the straight path. The material explains the verse as a description of the blessing of the Qur'an, which saves the reader from destruction and gives him the clearest path.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace."** The material explains that "the ways of peace" means the paths of safety and righteousness. It also explains that the Qur'an guides the one who seeks Allah's pleasure, so that the seeker is the one who receives the guidance. The material notes that peace here means the religion of Islam, and that the word peace is one of the names of Allah.

**"Brings them out of darkness and into light by His Will."** The darkness is disbelief and the light is faith. The material explains that the phrase "by His will" means by Allah's decree and by the success and grace He gives. The person who accepts the guidance is kept on it after he has accepted it.

**"And guides them to the Straight Path."** The material says the straight path is the religion of Islam, and that Allah keeps the believer on it. The guidance does not stop at the first step but continues to the end.

### The Qur'an as a blessing

The material says that the verse describes the Qur'an as a means of protecting people from what they fear, and of bringing them what they seek. It saves them from ruin and frees them from error. The verse therefore links the one who seeks Allah's pleasure with the one who receives the light, so that the approach to the Qur'an is itself a form of seeking Allah.

### In short

- The Qur'an guides those who seek Allah's pleasure to the ways of peace.
- It brings them out of darkness into light by Allah's will and keeps them on the straight path.

17.text:
"Indeed, those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have fallen into disbelief. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has the power to prevent Allah if He chose to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, his mother, and everyone in the world all together?” To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between. He creates whatever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything"

This verse refutes the belief that the Messiah, son of Mary, is Allah. It asks who could prevent Allah from destroying him, his mother, and everyone on earth, if Allah willed it. It then affirms that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone, that He creates what He wills, and that He is capable of everything. The material explains that the argument is aimed at a belief held by one group of Christians, but that it defeats the false belief of every group against the oneness of Allah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who say, ‘Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,’ have fallen into disbelief."** The material explains that the belief in question is the claim of one sect among the Christians, the Jacobites in one report. It says that the argument of the verse covers all of the false beliefs, whether that 'Isa is a son of God or that he is one of three gods.

**"Say, ‘Who has the power to prevent Allah if He chose to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, his mother, and everyone in the world all together?’"** The material explains that the question refutes the claim of divinity. If 'Isa were God, he could prevent his own destruction, but no one has the power to stop Allah. The material says that the mention of his mother is significant, because 'Isa and his mother both showed humility before Allah, and because the belief of one group that Maryam was one of three gods is also refuted by this mention. The material notes that the verse speaks of the death of 'Isa and of his mother as a supposition, even though Maryam had already died when the verse was revealed. The material explains that this is either because the point concerns 'Isa, or because the power that took her life is the same power that could take his.

**"To Allah alone belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between."** The material explains that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and that everything is under His power.

**"He creates whatever He wills."** The material explains that this refutes the reasoning that 'Isa must be divine because he was born without a father. Allah creates as He wills. The verse 3:59 says that the case of 'Isa in the sight of Allah is like the case of Adam, who was created without a father or a mother, and so the miraculous birth of 'Isa cannot make him God.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything."** The material says that Allah has the perfect and complete power to create as He wills, and that He is never asked about what He does.

### Power and creation

The material says that the verse answers a particular argument. The Christians reasoned that the birth of 'Isa, without a father, proved his divinity. The reply is that Allah created Adam without either father or mother, and that Allah's power is not limited by the ordinary course of nature. Creation shows the power of the Creator, and the creature is not divine because of how it came to be.

### In short

- Whoever says that the Messiah, son of Mary, is Allah has fallen into disbelief.
- No one can prevent Allah from destroying him, his mother, or anyone else, and this shows that they are all creatures.
- Allah creates what He wills, as He did with Adam, and this refutes the claim that a miraculous birth proves divinity.

18.text:
"The Jews and the Christians each say, “We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!” Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Why then does He punish you for your sins? No! You are only humans like others of His Own making. He forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills. To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between. And to Him is the final return.”"

This verse refutes a claim made by both the Jews and the Christians, that they are the children of Allah and His beloved. The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask them why Allah punishes them for their sins, if they are His beloved. The verse replies that they are only human beings, created like the rest, and that Allah forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. The material explains that the verse ends with the kingdom of Allah and with the return to Him.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Jews and the Christians each say, ‘We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!’"** The material explains that both communities made this claim. The Jews relied on a statement in their Scripture that Allah called Isra'il his firstborn, and they read it as a claim of special status. The Christians said that 'Isa called God his father, and they read it as a claim of sonship. The material says that the phrase can be read as a claim of closeness and honour, not of literal descent, but the verse rejects the claim in either sense.

**"Say, ‘Why then does He punish you for your sins?’"** The material explains that the question is a refutation. If the claim of sonship were true, the Fire would not be prepared for their disbelief and their lies. A father does not punish a beloved son in this way.

**"No! You are only humans like others of His Own making."** The material says that they are created as all of the children of Adam are created, and that Allah is the Lord of all His creation.

**"He forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills."** The material explains that Allah does as He wills, that no one can escape His judgment, and that He is swift in reckoning.

**"To Allah alone belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between. And to Him is the final return."** The material explains that everything is Allah's, and that the return of all people is to Him, when He will judge between His servants with justice.

### Claims of privilege

The material reads this verse as a warning against the belief that membership of a community brings special treatment. It says that earlier generations received blessings because of their deeds, but that later generations sometimes assume they are entitled to the same blessings simply because of their community. It says the verse removes this misunderstanding by showing that the consequences of conduct appear in this world, so that the people can see how Allah deals with them.

### In short

- The Jews and the Christians both claimed to be the children of Allah and His beloved.
- The verse refutes the claim by pointing to their sins and by stating that they are human beings, like others, whom Allah forgives or punishes as He wills.
- The verse also warns that no community is saved by its name alone, and that the return of all is to Allah.

19.text:
"O People of the Book! Our Messenger has indeed come to you, making things clear to you after an interval between the messengers so you do not say, “There has never come to us a deliverer of good news or a warner.” Now there has come to you a deliverer of good news and a warner. And Allah is Most Capable of everything"

This verse speaks to the People of the Book again. It says that Allah's Messenger has come to them, after a gap between the messengers, to make things clear. It gives the reason: so that they cannot say that no bringer of good news and no warner ever came to them. Then it confirms that a bringer of good news and a warner has now come, and it ends by saying that Allah is able to do all things. The material places the verse in the long gap between 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ, and it draws from that gap the honour of the Prophet's mission and the responsibility of those who received it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O People of the Book! Our Messenger has indeed come to you, making things clear to you."** The material explains that the address is to the Jews and the Christians, to the people of the Torah and the Gospel. The Messenger's task is to make clear the laws of religion, which had been obscured by changes to the Scriptures and by the passing of time.

**"After an interval between the messengers."** The material explains that the Arabic word fatrah means a period in which the sending of messengers has stopped. It identifies the interval as the time between 'Isa and the final Prophet. The material reports several figures for the length of this gap. Abu 'Uthman an-Nahdi and Qatadah are reported to have said it was six hundred years, and al-Bukhari records the same figure from Salman al-Farisi. Qatadah gave five hundred and sixty years and Ma'mar gave five hundred and forty. Others said six hundred and twenty. The material explains that the differences arise from counting in solar years or lunar years, since a hundred lunar years are about three years fewer than a hundred solar years. The gap is given as 569 years in the explanation of the translation, and the material notes that figure. It cites 18:25, where the People of the Cave are said to have stayed three hundred years and nine more, which the material reads as a lunar correction to the solar count that the People of the Book already knew.

The material says that the period was the time between the Children of Israel and the final Prophet, a time when prophets were absent from the world and the original religions had been altered. Idol worship, fire worship and the worship of the cross had spread, and evil and ignorance had covered the earth. The material notes that only a few remained loyal to the true teaching, among them some Jewish rabbis, Christian priests and Sabian monks. It presents the sending of the Prophet ﷺ as a blessing at the time when the world most needed it.

**"So you do not say, ‘There has never come to us a deliverer of good news or a warner.’"** The material explains that this is a warning against using the gap as an excuse. A people cannot say that no one came to warn them, once the Messenger has come. Ibn Jarir reads the part of the verse about Allah's power as meaning that Allah is able to punish those who disobey Him and to reward those who obey Him.

**"Now there has come to you a deliverer of good news and a warner."** The material says that the bringer of good news and the warner is Muhammad ﷺ. It explains that the Prophet is the last messenger after whom there will be no other.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything."** The material says that this phrase reminds the reader that Allah has the power to reward and to punish, so the warning is a serious one.

### The Prophet's place in the chain of messengers

The material cites the saying recorded by al-Bukhari, through Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said he had the greatest claim among all people on the son of Maryam, because there was no prophet between them. The material says this saying refutes the view of al-Qudai and others that a prophet named Khalid bin Sinan came after 'Isa. The material notes, however, that some reports on Khalid bin Sinan place him before 'Isa, and it leaves the matter at that.

The material also cites the long address that Iyad bin Himar al-Mujash'i reported from the Prophet ﷺ. In it, Allah says that He created all His servants as people who submit to the one God, that the devils led them away from their religion, and that Allah disliked the people of the earth except a few. The address says that Allah sent the Prophet ﷺ to test and to be tested, and that He sent him a Book that water cannot wash away. The material records this report and the mention of the Quraysh in it. It also says that Ahmad recorded the report, and that Muslim recorded part of it. Al-Mustafa, the chosen one, is one of the titles that the material uses for the Prophet ﷺ.

### Why the gap matters

The material draws a lesson from the gap. The Messenger came to a world that had lost its link with God, and the people he was sent to were proud, self-centred and resistant. Yet within a short time, these same people became teachers to the whole world in knowledge, conduct and morals. The material calls this proof that the Prophet ﷺ was truly the messenger of Allah, and it says that his teaching surpassed the teachings of all the earlier prophets. The comparison given is with a physician who heals a hopeless patient in a place that lacks medicine, and then turns the patient into a healer himself.

### The question of those who lived in the gap

The material discusses the fate of those who lived in the gap and never received a messenger or the law of an earlier prophet. Such people are excused and not punished, provided they did not commit shirk. The material says that most scholars hope that such people will be forgiven if they kept to what survived of the religion of Musa or 'Isa, and if they did not oppose the oneness of Allah. The reason is that the oneness of Allah can be known by reason, without a reported proof.

The material also raises a question. The People of the Book had their Torah and Gospel, so how could they plead ignorance? The answer given is that by the time of the Prophet ﷺ the original Scriptures had been lost, and the texts they had were altered. The material notes that Ibn Taymiyyah and others held that some original copies might have survived in places, but that this does not change the conclusion.

### A reminder that no community is favoured by name

The material reads the verse with a principle that one reading makes plain: no community is favoured in the eyes of Allah merely because of its name. Reckoning is individual. Each person is judged by his deeds in this world of trial, and Paradise and Hell are not the property of any group. Allah raises up warners and bringers of good news, and it is by supporting them and cooperating with them that a person finds Allah.

### In short

- The Messenger came after a gap in the sending of messengers, so that no one could plead that no warner had ever come.
- The gap lasted several hundred years by the reports the material gives, and the Prophet ﷺ came at a time of great need.
- The sending of the final messenger is a sign of Allah's mercy, and the reckoning is individual, not by community.

20.text:
"And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people, “O my people! Remember Allah’s favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign, and gave you what He had never given anyone in the world"

This verse begins the story of Musa and the Children of Israel. Musa reminds his people of three favours from Allah: prophets were raised up among them, they were made sovereign, and they were given what no one else in the world had been given. The material explains that the reminder was the preface to a command to enter the Holy Land. It places the verse in the chapter's wider call to remember the blessings of Allah and to answer them with obedience. The earlier verses had spoken of the covenant made with the twelve leaders, and this story shows how the covenant was tested.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And remember when Moses said to his people."** The material explains that Musa, to whom Allah spoke directly, reminded his people of what Allah had given them. He does this before he gives the command, which is the wise method of a teacher who first recalls the favours and then asks for the duty.

**"O my people! Remember Allah's favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you."** The material notes that there were many prophets among the Children of Israel, and that when one died another rose in his place, from the time of their forefather Ibrahim onward. The line ended with 'Isa, and the final prophet came from the offspring of Isma'il. The material calls this the most honoured of gifts, because it is a spiritual distinction that is hard to match. It cites a report from A'mash, recorded by Ibn Abi Hatim, that in one period alone a thousand prophets were sent to the Children of Israel between Musa and 'Isa.

**"Made you sovereign."** The material explains the word translated as sovereign. It reports that 'Abdur-Razzaq recorded Ibn 'Abbas saying that the favour was a servant, a wife and a house. Al-Hakim recorded that Ibn 'Abbas said it was a wife and a servant, and Qatadah said they were the first people to keep servants. The material says the word "kings" is applied to the whole people, in the sense that every one of them owned a home and household, or in the sense that a people who have a ruler are known as rulers by proxy. One reading takes this as a hint that an Islamic state is run by the people, who elect their leader and can remove him by their collective will.

**"And gave you what He had never given anyone in the world."** The material explains that the phrase means what was given in their own time, and that they were the most honoured people of their age. It cites 45:16, which says that Allah gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, the wisdom and the prophethood, and preferred them above the nations. It also cites 7:138-140, where Musa told the people that he would not seek a god for them other than Allah, who had preferred them over the nations.

### The favour and the test

The material says the favour carried a test. The people who had been slaves of Pharaoh had seen Allah destroy their enemy and make them masters of Egypt. They had seen the sea divided and the drowning of Pharaoh and his army. Yet the verses that follow show that they still refused the command. The material says this shows that favour without gratitude does not protect a people from disobedience.

The material also notes that the earlier community was given many favours, and that the Muslim ummah has its own status. It cites 2:143, which describes the Muslim community as a moderate nation, and it notes that the reports about the honour of this community are many. The material answers the apparent contradiction by saying that the blessing spoken of in this verse is limited to the time of Musa.

### In short

- Musa reminded his people of three favours: the prophets among them, their sovereignty, and what no one else had been given.
- The favours were a preface to a command, and they were given so that the people would obey.
- The verse teaches that favour from Allah must be answered with gratitude and obedience.

21.text:
"O my people! Enter the Holy Land which Allah has destined for you ˹to enter˺. And do not turn back or else you will become losers.”"

This verse gives the command. Musa tells his people to enter the Holy Land that Allah has destined for them, and not to turn back, because turning back would make them losers. The material identifies the Holy Land with Syria, and it explains that the command came with good news of victory, since the land had been promised to them.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O my people! Enter the Holy Land which Allah has destined for you."** The material explains that the Holy Land is Syria, and it cites Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said that he had read in the Torah that Syria is a special treasure of Allah on earth, with His dear servants in it. The material explains that the Holy Land is Syria, and that some reports identify it with Jerusalem, Palestine, Jordan or Damascus. Qatadah is reported to have said that the whole of Syria is the Holy Land. The material says the land is holy because it was the home of many prophets. It also notes a report that Ibrahim, looking from a mountain in Lebanon, was told that the land he could see was the Holy Land. The material says that the different reports do not really conflict, since the reports describe different parts of one land.

**"And do not turn back or else you will become losers."** The material explains that turning back means retreating from the jihad. The loss is the loss of the promised land and of the favour that goes with it.

### The promise attached to the command

The material says that the command came with a promise, and that the jihad it called for was the way the Children of Israel were to take what was theirs. The land had been given to the believers among them through their forefather Isra'il, and Musa had received the assurance of victory. The verse therefore asks the people to act on a promise that Allah had already given. The material says that Musa's wise method was to recall the favours first, then to give the command, and then to remind them of the promise.

### In short

- Allah had destined the Holy Land for the Children of Israel, and Musa commanded them to enter it.
- They were warned not to turn back, because turning back would make them losers.
- The command came with a promise, so the people had no reason to doubt the outcome.

22.text:
"They replied, “O Moses! There is an enormously powerful people there, so we will never ˹be able to˺ enter it until they leave. If they do, then we will enter!”"

This verse gives the reply of the people. They say that the land is held by an enormously powerful people, and that they will never enter until those people leave. The material explains that the people were afraid of the Amalekites who held the land, and it notes that the reply was a refusal in the form of a condition.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They replied, ‘O Moses! There is an enormously powerful people there.’"** The material explains that the enemy were the Amalekites, who were said to be of the people of 'Ad. The material reports that Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Abi Talhah said that they were unusually tall and strong. The material notes that many stories were told about their size, but the scholars it follows hold that these tales have no basis in reason or in the law, and that the strength of the Amalekites was the subject of the common report. The Amalekites were the remnant of the people of 'Ad, and they held Syria and Jerusalem at the time of the Children of Israel, who were the Bani Isra'il of this story and the Pharaoh had been their oppressor earlier.

**"So we will never be able to enter it until they leave."** The material says that the people refused the command outright. They presented their fear as the reason, and they set a condition that they could never meet on their own.

**"If they do, then we will enter!"** The material explains that the people did not intend to fight at all. They wanted the enemy to leave the land, so that they could enter it without a battle. This was a refusal to obey Musa.

### The weakness of the reply

The material says that the reply shows a people who had seen clear signs of Allah's power but still lacked trust in Him. It contrasts their reply with the response of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and the Ansar at Badr, who were ready to fight. The material says that a reply of this kind is what breaks faith with a prophet, even when it is not a formal rejection.

### In short

- The people said the enemy was too powerful to face, and they set a condition that would never be met.
- The reply was a refusal to obey, and it showed a lack of trust in Allah's promise.
- The material contrasts it with the readiness of the believers at Badr.

23.text:
"Two God-fearing men—who had been blessed by Allah—said, “Surprise them through the gate. If you do, you will certainly prevail. Put your trust in Allah if you are ˹truly˺ believers.”"

This verse gives the counsel of two men who feared Allah. They tell the people to surprise the enemy through the gate, and they promise that victory will follow. They end by telling the people to put their trust in Allah, if they are truly believers. The material identifies the two men as Yusha' bin Nun and Kalib bin Yufanna, who had kept the secret of the reconnaissance mission, while the others had disclosed it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Two God-fearing men, who had been blessed by Allah."** The material explains that the two men are described in two ways. The first is that they feared Allah, and the material says this means they feared Allah alone, because no one else can bring benefit or harm without His will. The second is that Allah had blessed them. The material says that any excellence a person has is a blessing from Allah. Twelve chiefs had been sent to spy on the enemy, and only these two kept faith with Musa's instruction not to reveal what they had seen.

**"Surprise them through the gate. If you do, you will certainly prevail."** The material explains that the advice was to advance boldly on the city gate. The two men may have judged, from their own assessment of the Amalekites, that they were strong in body but weak in heart, and that a surprise attack would break them. The material also says the men may have spoken from their faith in the promise of Allah that Musa had told them.

**"Put your trust in Allah if you are truly believers."** The material says that trust in Allah is what the believer relies on after taking the means, and that Allah's custom is to give victory after faith and preparation. Allah gives the reward to those who act, and the trust is the condition of the action.

### The story of the spies

The material gives an account of the spies. The twelve chiefs went ahead to Jerusalem and were captured by the Amalekites, who then freed them. When they reported back, most of them spoke of the strength of the enemy, and the people were frightened. The material says that the two men were Caleb and Yusha', and that the people of the Bani Isra'il were afraid to go to the Syrian land. Musa had asked the spies to keep their findings secret, but ten of them let it out. Only Yusha' and Kalib, whom the material also calls Caleb, kept the secret and reported faithfully to the ummah. The material says that these two men were the ones who spoke in the verse.

### In short

- Two men who feared Allah urged the people to advance through the gate, with trust in Allah.
- They had kept faith with Musa, while the others had spread fear.
- The verse teaches that victory follows faith joined with action.

24.text:
"˹Yet˺ they said, “O Moses! ˹Still˺ we will never enter as long as they remain there. So go—both you and your Lord—and fight; we are staying right here!”"

This verse gives the final refusal of the people. Even after the counsel of the two men, they say that they will never enter while the enemy is in the land. They tell Musa to go with his Lord and fight, while they stay where they are. The material says this reply was a grave refusal, and it became proverbial.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Yet they said, ‘O Moses! Still we will never enter as long as they remain there.’"** The material explains that the word "still" shows that they had heard the advice and rejected it. Their repeated refusal shows that they had no intention of obeying.

**"So go, both you and your Lord, and fight; we are staying right here."** The material explains that the reply could be read as mockery, which would be disbelief. The material says that the more likely meaning is that they meant "you go and fight, your Lord will help you, but we will not help you." Even so, the response was rude and grotesque. The material notes that this statement became a proverb about those who refuse to act.

### The companions at Badr

The material places this reply beside the response of the Companions at Badr. The Prophet ﷺ prayed to Allah before the battle, and Miqdad bin al-Aswad said that they would never say to the Prophet what the Children of Israel had said to Musa. He said they would defend him from the right, the left, the front and the back. The Prophet ﷺ was pleased, and Ibn Mas'ud is reported to have said that he envied Miqdad's words. The material also records Sa'd bin Mu'adh's reply at Badr, which was part of the jihad of the early ummah,, and the report of the Ansar, who said that they would follow the Prophet even if he led them to the camels at Bark al-Ghimad near Makkah. Imam Ahmad, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Hibban recorded this report, and al-Bukhari recorded Miqdad's words.

### In short

- The people refused a third time, and their refusal was a breach of the pledge they had given.
- The material says the reply was grave but not open blasphemy, that it became a proverb, and that Musa was still living among them and praying for them, which would not have been possible if the words were open blasphemy. The material says the one who refuses to join the jihad breaks the pledge he has given.
- The Companions at Badr gave the opposite reply, pledging to stand with the Prophet.

25.text:
"Moses pleaded, “My Lord! I have no control over anyone except myself and my brother. So set us apart from the rebellious people.”"

This verse gives Musa's prayer. After his people had refused to enter the Holy Land and had said that they would sit where they were while he and his Lord fought, Musa turns to Allah. He says that he has no control over anyone except himself and his brother, and he asks Allah to set them apart from the rebellious people. The material reads the prayer as the cry of a prophet who has been worn down by the repeated breaches of his people, and who asks only for what he can rely on.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Moses pleaded, ‘My Lord!’"** The material says that Musa was very angry with the Children of Israel when they refused to fight, and that he turned to his Lord in supplication against them. The word "pleaded" in the translation captures the urgency of the prayer.

**"I have no control over anyone except myself and my brother."** The material explains that Musa speaks of himself and his brother Harun, because they alone among the people would obey and carry out Allah's command. The material notes that Harun was a prophet, and was protected from error, so Musa could be sure of his steadfastness. It also says that the two righteous men, Yusha' and Kalib, were not spoken of, since they were not protected from error in the same way. The material says that Musa's words reflect his pain at the treachery of his people, and that the same disobedience was the cause of what he said.

**"So set us apart from the rebellious people."** The material reports several readings of this phrase. Ibn 'Abbas, through al-'Awfi and 'Ali bin Abi Talhah, said it means judge between us and them. Ad-Dahhak said it means judge and decide. Others said it means separate between us and them. The material notes that the request is for the people to receive what they deserve, and for Musa and Harun to receive what they deserve, so that the two groups are not mixed.

### The prophet's pain and the reply

The material says that the prayer shows a prophet who has done everything he could for his people. He had freed them from slavery, shown them the signs of Allah, and led them out of Egypt. Yet they still refused the command. The material says that the prophets feel the disobedience of their people deeply, and that this is part of their nature. It also notes that Musa's trust in Allah is complete, and that he turns to Allah alone once human means have failed.

The material also contrasts the people's reply with the readiness of the Companions at Badr, who pledged to defend the Prophet ﷺ from every side. The contrast is the same one that the earlier verses drew, and this verse closes the scene of the refusal.

### In short

- Musa prayed to Allah after his people refused to enter the Holy Land.
- He asked for judgment and separation between himself and the rebellious people, because he had no power over them beyond himself and his brother.
- The prayer shows a prophet who has done all he could and who turns in trust to Allah.

26.text:
"Allah replied, “Then this land is forbidden to them for forty years, during which they will wander through the land. So do not grieve for the rebellious people.”"

This verse gives Allah's reply to Musa. The land is forbidden to the people for forty years, during which they will wander aimlessly across the land. Allah tells Musa not to grieve for the rebellious people. The material explains that the forbidden land was Syria, and that the people were kept in a small open area, moving in circles, until a new generation grew up and entered the land under Yusha'.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah replied, ‘Then this land is forbidden to them for forty years.’"** The material explains that the land of Syria was forbidden to them for forty years. They could not go there, and they could not return to Egypt either. They were kept in the wilderness of al-Tih. The material explains that the punishment fitted the offence. Because they had said "we will sit here," they were kept sitting in the wilderness for forty years.

**"During which they will wander through the land."** The material says that the wandering was a confinement without walls. The people walked all day, expecting to reach Egypt or Syria, and by evening they were back where they had started.
