The material notes that the area was small, and that the people, numbering several hundred thousand by one account, were held within it until the older generation died. The material says Allah does not need prisons. The whole creation is under His command, and when He wills to hold someone, the air, the earth and the open land become the jailer.

**"So do not grieve for the rebellious people."** The material explains that Allah is comforting Musa, and that the prophets are naturally moved by the suffering of their people even when it is deserved. Musa is told not to grieve over the punishment, because the people had earned it through their own rebellion.

### What the forty years held

The material says that the forty years were not only a punishment. During this time Allah gave the people clouds for shade, manna and quails for food, water from a rock struck with Musa's staff, and light by night. The material notes that these blessings came because of the presence of Musa and Harun, and perhaps because some of the people repented. It says that the Torah was revealed in this period, and that the Covenant was established for the Children of Israel.

The material says that Harun died during the forty years, and that Musa died soon after, and that Allah then raised Yusha' bin Nun as a prophet. When the forty years were over, Yusha' led the remaining people toward Jerusalem, and the land was conquered. The material notes that the conquest was in fulfilment of the promise that Allah had made, and that the generation who refused the command did not enter it. The material also relates that the sun was held back for Yusha' on the Friday when the conquest was completed, so that he could finish before the Sabbath began.

### The lesson of the wilderness

The material draws the lesson that the people were more afraid of men than of Allah, and that this fear cost them the land. It says that the promise was fulfilled through a new generation that had grown up in the hardship of the desert. It also says that the verse 5:21 and 5:22 show the fear of the people, and this verse shows its consequence. The material notes that the chapter speaks to the believers so that they will not repeat the same fear.

### In short

- The land was forbidden to the people for forty years, and they wandered in a small area until the older generation had died.
- The forty years were a punishment, but they also held blessings, through the presence of Musa and Harun.
- The promise was fulfilled through a new generation under Yusha', and the verse teaches that fear of people can cost a community what Allah has given it.

27.text:
"Relate to them in truth ˹O Prophet˺ the story of Adam’s two sons—how each offered a sacrifice: Abel’s offering was accepted while Cain’s was not. So Cain threatened, “I will kill you!” His brother replied, “Allah only accepts ˹the offering˺ of the sincerely devout"

This verse begins the story of the two sons of Adam, Habil (Abel) and Qabil (Cain). The Prophet ﷺ is told to recount it truthfully. Each brother offered a sacrifice to Allah, and only Habil's was accepted. Qabil threatened to kill him, and Habil replied that Allah accepts only from those who are God-fearing. The material explains that the story is told as a lesson about envy, injustice and the acceptance of deeds, and that it is set against the earlier account of the cowardice of the Children of Israel. The story condemns unjust killing and shows that its consequences are severe in this life and the next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Relate to them in truth, O Prophet, the story of Adam's two sons."** The material explains that the word "truth" is a principle for every historical account. The narrative must have nothing false in it, nothing dubious, and nothing added or removed. The material cites the same word of truth in other places: 3:62, about the account of 'Isa, and 18:13 and 19:43, where the account of the people of the cave and of 'Isa are called true. It also cites 19:34, where 'Isa is described as a word of truth. The material says the Qur'an's careful choice of the word truth shows that a narrator must be exact. It also argues that the Prophet ﷺ, who could not read or write, told these events exactly, which is evidence that the revelation came from Allah.

The material notes that most authorities take "the two sons of Adam" to mean the two real sons, Habil and Qabil, though the words could also cover every human being descended from Adam. The Companions and early scholars are reported to have said that the account is meant for the envious and unjust among the people.

**"How each offered a sacrifice: Abel's offering was accepted while Cain's was not."** The material explains that the sacrifice was made to draw nearer to Allah. The sign of acceptance was a fire from the sky that consumed the offering, and an offering that was not consumed remained unaccepted. Habil owned flocks and offered the best of a spring lamb. Qabil was a farmer and offered grain. The fire consumed Habil's offering and left Qabil's untouched. The material gives the background: at that time every child of Adam was born as a twin, a son and a daughter, and marriage was allowed between a son of one birth and a daughter of another. The beautiful daughter of one birth was to marry the son of the other, and Qabil wanted the beautiful sister for himself. Adam proposed the offering as a way of settling the dispute.

**"So Cain threatened, 'I will kill you!'"** The material says that the threat came from envy, after the failure had shamed him. It cites the report that envy is the cause of the threat, because Habil had received a blessing that Qabil had not.

**"His brother replied, 'Allah only accepts the offering of the sincerely devout.'"** The material explains that Habil answered with a principle: acceptance depends on taqwa. If Qabil had been God-fearing, his offering would have been accepted. The material says this also contains the cure for envy. When a person sees another blessed, he should look at his own shortcomings and repent, not wish to take the blessing away.

### Acceptance depends on sincerity and taqwa

The material draws the principle of the verse out in full. Deeds are accepted only when they come from taqwa and sincerity. The material cites Ibn Mas'ud, who said that if he were certain Allah had accepted one of his deeds, he would not give it up for the whole world. It cites Abu al-Darda', who said that one accepted prayer would be better for him than the world and all in it. It also cites 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, who wrote that no deed is accepted without taqwa, and 'Ali, who said that a deed done with taqwa is never small. The material also says that 'Amir ibn 'Abdullah wept at death, because he did not know whether his worship had been accepted.

### In short

- The story of Habil and Qabil is to be told truthfully, as the Qur'an tells the stories of 'Isa and of the cave.
- The sacrifice of Habil was accepted because of his taqwa, and Qabil's was not.
- Habil's reply gives the principle that deeds are accepted only from the God-fearing, and it is also a cure for envy.

28.text:
"If you raise your hand to kill me, I will not raise mine to kill you, because I fear Allah—the Lord of all worlds"

This verse gives Habil's reply to the threat. If Qabil raises his hand to kill him, Habil will not raise his hand against Qabil. He gives his reason: he fears Allah, the Lord of all the worlds. The material says that Habil was the stronger of the two, but fear of Allah restrained him. The material links the verse to a saying of the Prophet ﷺ about two Muslims who meet with swords, and to the teaching on patience in the face of fitnah.

### Phrase by phrase

**"If you raise your hand to kill me."** The material notes that Habil did not reply with anger. He spoke with peace and principle, and he had sympathy for his brother.

**"I will not raise mine to kill you."** The material explains that Habil refused to imitate the crime. He did not want to earn the same sin as his brother. He chose patience and endurance.

**"Because I fear Allah, the Lord of all worlds."** The material says that fear of Allah stopped Habil's hand, and that the only being worthy of fear is Allah, since no one can benefit or harm without His will. Abdullah bin 'Amr is reported to have said that Habil was the stronger, but his fear of Allah restrained his hand.

### The teaching on killing between believers

The material cites the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, recorded in the Two Sahihs, that when two Muslims meet with their swords, both the killer and the killed will be in the Fire. The Companions asked about the one who was killed, and the Prophet ﷺ said that he too had intended to kill his companion. The material cites Sa'd bin Abi Waqqas, who, at the start of the trouble that befell 'Uthman, reported that the Prophet ﷺ said it is better to sit idle in a time of fitnah than to stand up in it. When asked what to do if someone enters one's home to kill him, Sa'd reported that the Prophet ﷺ said to be like the pious son of Adam. At-Tirmidhi recorded this, with similar reports from Abu Hurayrah, Khabbab, Abu Bakr, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Waqid and Abu Musa.

### In short

- Habil refused to raise his hand against his brother, because he feared Allah.
- The material says that fear of Allah, not weakness, restrained him.
- The verse teaches that a believer must not answer the threat of killing with killing, and that restraint is better in a time of fitnah.

29.text:
"I want to let you bear your sin against me along with your other sins, then you will be one of those destined to the Fire. And that is the reward of the wrongdoers.”"

This verse gives the rest of Habil's reply. He says that he would rather Qabil bear the sin of killing him, along with his other sins, so that he would be among the people of the Fire. It ends by saying that this is the reward of the wrongdoers. The material explains that this is a warning, and that Habil's statement is not a wish for the Fire, but a statement of what the crime would bring.

### Phrase by phrase

**"I want to let you bear your sin against me along with your other sins."** The material says that Habil, whom the story calls Abel, is speaking. The material explains that the words mean the sin of killing Habil, added to Qabil's earlier sins. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi and Qatadah are reported to have said the same. The material notes that Habil does not wish to take on that burden himself.

**"Then you will be one of those destined to the Fire."** The material says that the Fire is the place of the one who commits this crime. Habil is describing the end of his brother's path, not praying for it.

**"And that is the reward of the wrongdoers."** The material explains that this is the general rule: those who wrongfully transgress are rewarded with the Fire. The verse makes a general principle out of the particular case.

### The burden of unjust killing

The material says that Adam's first son carries a share of every unjust killing that follows, because he was the first to commit murder. It cites a saying recorded by Ahmad and the group of collectors, except Abu Dawud, and a report of 'Abdullah bin 'Amr, who said that the son of Adam who killed his brother would be the most wretched of men. The material says that a sin of killing brings punishment in this world as well, and that transgression and cutting the ties of kinship are sins that are punished quickly.

### In short

- Habil told his brother that he would rather bear no share in the sin, and that the killer would carry the sin of the killing with his other sins.
- The reward of wrongdoers is the Fire, and this verse states the general rule.
- The first murderer carries a share in every unjust killing that follows, and the punishment for such crimes begins in this life.

30.text:
"Yet Cain convinced himself to kill his brother, so he killed him—becoming a loser"

This verse tells what Qabil did. His self urged him on, and he killed his brother, and so he became one of the losers. The material explains that the verse shows the inner struggle that leads a person to crime, and that the loss he suffered was both in this life and in the next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Yet Cain convinced himself to kill his brother."** The material explains that Qabil's self made the killing seem reasonable. The material notes that Shaytan played a part in the crime, and that Adam, in the account, was the father of both men. One report says that Shaytan showed Qabil how to kill, by placing an animal's head on a rock and crushing it with another stone, and that Qabil did the same to his brother. A report from Zayd bin Aslam, passed on by his son 'Abdur-Rahman, says that Qabil was twisting his brother's neck, not knowing how to kill him, until Shaytan told him to strike his head with a stone.

**"So he killed him, becoming a loser."** The material explains that Qabil lost in this life and in the next, and that no loss is greater than this. The material also notes that Qabil did not know what to do with the body, and carried it on his back because he was the first person to die on earth.

### The voice of conscience

The material reads the verse with the teaching of conscience. A question arising in a person's conscience is a test. A person who answers the voice of conscience succeeds, and a person who hides behind false excuses to silence it fails. The material says that Qabil first felt that his action was unjustified, but his envy did not cool, and he invented reasons until he found rest in them and killed his brother.

The material also says that the verse shows the path of sin. A man who buries his bad intention in his heart does not have to bury a body afterwards.

### In short

- Qabil's self urged him to kill his brother, and he did so.
- He became one of the losers, both in this life and the next.
- The verse teaches that the conscience is a test, and that a person who silences it with excuses has failed.

31.text:
"Then Allah sent a crow digging ˹a grave˺ in the ground ˹for a dead crow˺, in order to show him how to bury the corpse of his brother. He cried, “Alas! Have I ˹even˺ failed to be like this crow and bury the corpse of my brother?” So he became regretful"

This verse tells how Allah taught Qabil what to do with his brother's body. He sent a crow that dug a grave for another dead crow, and Qabil learned how to bury his brother. He cried out that he had failed to be like the crow, and he became regretful. The material says that the regret came after the crime, not before, and that the animal taught the man a lesson in how to bury the dead.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Then Allah sent a crow digging a grave for a dead crow."** The material explains that Qabil did not know how to bury his brother. Several reports say that two crows fought, one killed the other, and the living crow dug a grave and buried the dead one. Ibn 'Abbas is reported to have said that a crow came to a dead crow and covered it with sand until it was hidden in the ground.

### Regret after the crime

**"In order to show him how to bury the corpse of his brother."** The material explains that the lesson was practical. The animal taught the man, and the material draws the point that a person can know less than a bird about burying the dead. One reading says Qabil had to bury his brother's naked body, and the material notes that the lesson concerned covering the body.

### The lesson of the crow

**"He cried, 'Alas! Have I even failed to be like this crow and bury the corpse of my brother?'"** The material explains that Qabil was sorry that he had failed to do what the crow had done, but was not sorry for the killing itself. The material says that his regret was for his inability to bury his brother, not for his crime.

**"So he became regretful."** The material says that al-Hasan al-Basri explained the regret as Allah making him feel sorrow for the loss he had earned. The material notes that regret is the end of those who commit sins.

### In short

- Allah taught Qabil how to bury his brother by sending a crow to bury another crow.
- Qabil regretted his failure to bury his brother, but his regret was not for the killing itself.
- The verse shows that regret follows sin, and that the lesson came from an animal.

32.text:
"That is why We ordained for the Children of Israel that whoever takes a life—unless as a punishment for murder or mischief in the land—it will be as if they killed all of humanity; and whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity. ˹Although˺ Our messengers already came to them with clear proofs, many of them still transgressed afterwards through the land"

This verse draws a rule from the story of the two sons of Adam in 5:27 to 5:31. Because of the crime of Qabil, Allah prescribed for the Children of Israel that taking a life is as if one had killed all of mankind, unless it is a punishment for murder or for corruption in the land. Saving a life is as if one had saved all of mankind. The verse then says that messengers came to them with clear proofs, but many of them still transgressed in the land. The material reads the verse as a general principle of the sanctity of human life, and as a warning against the disorder that unjust killing brings. It is the central legal rule of this part of the chapter.

### Phrase by phrase

**"That is why We ordained for the Children of Israel."** The material says the phrase "that is why" links the rule to the crime of Qabil. The material also notes that the Qur'an tells such stories with the word truth, as it does for the people of the cave in 18:13 and for 'Isa, son of Maryam, in 19:34, so that the account of Qabil is given with the same care. The killing of Habil was the first unjust killing, and the rule that follows is given to the Children of Israel as a law. The material notes that Allah legislated for them and informed them of it. It also notes that the rule was not peculiar to them, since the same principle applies to all people.

**"Whoever takes a life, unless as a punishment for murder or mischief in the land, it will be as if they killed all of humanity."** The material explains that a life may be taken only in two cases: as retribution for murder, or as the punishment for spreading mischief in the land. Any other killing is treated as the killing of all mankind, because one life is not worth less than another in its sanctity. The material gives several explanations of this comparison. Mujahid said that whoever kills a believer intentionally will be cursed, and that his punishment is the same as if he had killed all people. Ibn 'Abbas explained that whoever kills one soul whose killing Allah has forbidden is like one who kills all mankind. Sa'id bin Jubayr said that whoever allows the blood of one Muslim to be shed is like one who allows the blood of all people to be shed.

The material cites a report from Abu Hurayrah, who went to 'Uthman while he was besieged, to offer his support. 'Uthman asked him whether he would like to kill all the people, including him. Abu Hurayrah said no. 'Uthman said that killing one man is the same as killing all, and he told him to go back without fighting.

**"Whoever saves a life, it will be as if they saved all of humanity."** The material explains that saving a life means refraining from killing a soul that Allah has forbidden to kill. Whoever forbids the killing of one soul without justice protects the lives of all people from himself. Mujahid is reported to have said that whoever kills no one, the lives of people are safe from him. Sa'id bin Jubayr is also reported to have said that whoever forbids the shedding of the blood of one Muslim is like one who forbids the shedding of the blood of all people.

**"Although Our messengers already came to them with clear proofs."** The material explains that the clear proofs are the signs and evidence brought by the messengers. The verse criticises those who transgress after knowing that a thing is forbidden. The material mentions the case of the Jews of Madinah, including the tribes of Qurayzah, an-Nadir and Qaynuqa', who used to fight alongside Khazraj or Aws in the days before Islam. When the war ended, they would ransom the captives of the other side, even though they had themselves killed. Allah criticised this in Surat al-Baqarah, in 2:84-85, which says that they shed one another's blood and drove out their own people, and then ransomed the captives, although their expulsion was forbidden to them.

**"Many of them still transgressed afterwards through the land."** The material explains that the transgression is the spread of mischief and disorder. The word translated transgress covers unbelief, killing and similar crimes, and the material says that the mischief in the land covers many kinds of evil.

### The punishment for mischief in the land

The material explains the verses that come after this one, since the rule about mischief in the land has its own punishment. It cites 5:33, which says that those who wage war against Allah and His messenger and spread corruption in the land shall be killed, crucified, have their hands and feet cut off on opposite sides, or be banished from the land. The material says that the choice indicated by "or" is a choice for the ruler, as it is in the other places where the Qur'an uses the same word, including the penalty for killing game in the sacred state in 5:95. The material reports that Ibn 'Abbas took the verse to mean that a person who takes up arms in the land of Islam and spreads fear on the roads, if he is caught, may be killed, crucified, or have his hands and feet cut off. It reports that Sa'id bin al-Musayyib, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibrahim an-Nakha'i and ad-Dahhak said something similar.

The material notes that the verses were read by some as referring to the idolaters, and by others as general. It says that the more reliable view is that the verse is general. It reports the account of a group from the tribe of 'Ukl, who killed a herdsman, drove away the camels, and were punished severely after they had been healed by drinking the milk and urine of the camels. The material says this is the basis of the punishment in the verse.

The material also states that the punishment does not apply to a person who repents before he is caught. Ibn Jarir, reporting from 'Ikrimah and al-Hasan al-Basri, and the material on Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Dawud, says the early reports of the verse were read as applying to the idolaters who repented before capture, and that later views held the same for Muslims. The material gives the case of 'Ali al-Asadi, who waged war and shed blood, then repented after hearing a verse that tells the believers not to despair of the mercy of Allah. He went to Madinah, sat with Abu Hurayrah, and Marwan was told that he had come in repentance and could not be punished. He went to sea in jihad, and the account says that the ship he was on drowned with the enemy.

### The reports on the sanctity of life

The material cites 'Ubadah bin as-Samit, who reported that the Prophet ﷺ took the same pledge from the men as he did from the women, that they would not associate anything with Allah, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, or spread lies. Whoever keeps the pledge has his reward with Allah. Whoever falls short and is punished has his punishment as expiation. Whoever is covered by Allah's forgiveness is in Allah's hands. The material also cites a report from 'Ali, recorded by Ahmad, Ibn Majah and at-Tirmidhi, that Allah is far more just than to punish a servant twice for one sin, and far more generous than to punish him for a fault He has pardoned. Ad-Daraqutni said that the report is sound in its attribution to the Prophet ﷺ.

### In short

- Unjust killing is as if one had killed all mankind, and saving a life is as if one had saved all mankind.
- Killing is allowed only as retribution for murder or as punishment for corruption in the land, and the punishment for corruption is set out in 5:33.
- The verse is also a warning against transgression after clear proofs, and it gives the example of those who repent before capture.

33.text:
"Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land is death, crucifixion, cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile from the land. This ˹penalty˺ is a disgrace for them in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter"

This verse sets out the punishment for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land. The material explains that the verse describes armed robbery and banditry, where a group uses force to break the law of the land and to make people afraid. The punishment is death, crucifixion, cutting of the hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile. The verse says the penalty is a disgrace in this world and a great punishment in the Hereafter. The verse follows the story of the two sons of Adam and the rule against unjust killing in 5:32, and it moves from the principle to its enforcement.

The material treats this verse as the heart of the Islamic law of crimes against public safety. It explains the three kinds of punishment in the law, the difference between the rights of Allah and the rights of people, and why the punishment for this crime is fixed.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, the penalty for those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger and spread mischief in the land."** The material explains that the word for waging war comes from a root meaning to seize or snatch, and it is the opposite of peace and security. The war in view is the spreading of disorder. Isolated theft or a single killing does not disturb public peace. The verse concerns a powerful and organised group that robs and kills by force and breaks the law of the land. This is the reading of the Muslim jurists. The material says that the phrase "against Allah and His Messenger" is used because a group that breaks the law of Allah with force is at war with the government, and where the government is Islamic, that war is against Allah and His Messenger, even though the victims are ordinary people.

The material explains the difference between two words. Muqatalah is a bloody fight, and Muharabah is group-led intrusion into life, property and honour by force. The verse uses the second word. Muharabah includes highway robbery, rebellion, and attacks on property, honour and life.

**"Is death, crucifixion, cutting off their hands and feet on opposite sides, or exile from the land."** The material explains that these are four punishments, linked by the word "or". The word is read in two ways. Some early authorities and Imam Malik held that the ruler has the choice among the four, depending on the power of the robbers and the gravity of the crime. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal read the word as dividing the punishments among different kinds of crime. They supported this with a report from Ibn 'Abbas, which tells of a peace treaty with Abu Burdah al-Aslami, who broke it by robbing people on their way to Madinah to embrace Islam. The angel Jibril brought the rule that whoever killed and robbed should be crucified, whoever killed but did not rob should be killed, whoever robbed but did not kill should have his hand and foot cut off, and whoever only spread fear should be exiled. Anyone who repents before being taken is excused.

The material also notes that the three punishments of killing, crucifixion and cutting are written in a grammatical form that expresses repetition and intensity. It also notes that the plural form applies to the whole group, even when only one of them committed the crime, because they all shared the plan. The punishment is therefore a Hadd, the right of Allah, not a Qisas that the victim could forgive.

The material also reports the view of 'Umar al-Faruq about exile: a man who is exiled but left free to roam will harass the people of other towns, so it is better to imprison him. Abu Hanifah took this view.

**"This penalty is a disgrace for them in this world."** The material says that the punishment brings humiliation in this life, and that the Hereafter punishment is harsher and more lasting. It also says that the worldly punishment does not remove the Hereafter punishment unless the person sincerely repents.

### The three kinds of punishment in the law

The material explains the law's three kinds of punishment. The Hudud are fixed punishments for crimes that are a right of Allah. There are five: robbery, theft, adultery, false accusation of adultery, and the drinking of wine. The Qisas is retaliation for killing or wounding, which is a right of the person harmed, and so the victim or his guardian can forgive it. The Ta'zir are penalties left to the judge, and they can range from light to severe or be pardoned. A Hadd cannot be waived by a ruler, and it cannot be reduced by repentance once the crime is proved in court, although the Hereafter punishment can be forgiven by sincere repentance. A Hadd is dropped in case of doubt, but the offender is not left unpunished, and the judge may give a lesser penalty.

### Robbery and the rights of people

The material says that a repentance does not remove the rights of the servants of Allah. Anything taken must be returned, and where someone was killed or wounded, the rule of Qisas applies, which the heirs may forgive. Abu Hanifah and most jurists hold that the financial liability must be discharged or forgiven. A robber is considered truly repentant only when he pays for the rights he violated, or they are forgiven.

### Who is included, and the cases the reports give

The material says that the verse applies to a group or individual who robs people and breaks the law by force of arms. It does not include common individual thieves or pickpockets, who fall under the rules for theft. Some reports tie the verse to a particular occasion. One account, from Anas and recorded by Muslim, speaks of a group from the tribes of Ukl and Uraynah who came to Madinah ill, and were told to go out with the Prophet's herd and drink its milk and urine. When they recovered, they killed the shepherd, drove off the camels, and were brought back and punished severely. Another reading names the Arniyyun, who came to Madinah ill, were treated in the same way, killed the shepherd and stole the herd. Qatadah is reported to have said that the verse was revealed about them. The material does not settle the detail, but it treats the case as the setting of the rule.

A further account concerns the people of Hilal bin 'Uwaymir, who killed a group of travellers from the Banu Kinanah who had been on their way to Madinah to declare their Islam. The material says the verse was read by some as a judgement on idolators who killed and looted, and it sets out the same four punishments for each kind of crime.

The material also reports the view of Sa'id bin al-Musayyib, 'Ata', Dawud, al-Hasan al-Basri, ad-Dahhak, an-Nakha'i and Mujahid, who took the choice to be the ruler's, and it notes that the Imam Malik held the same view. Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal, with a group of Companions and Successors, read the word as dividing the punishments among the crimes.

### The grammar and the group

The material says that the first three punishments in the verse use a verbal form that expresses repetition and intensity, and that the plural applies to the whole group, so that the punishment falls on all, although one member did the act. The material says this shows that the punishment is a Hadd, a right of Allah, and not a retaliation that the victim may forgive. The form also shows that the crime is the group's, since they all acted in the cooperation of their companions.

The material explains the sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ as the basis for these rules, and the consensus of the Companions on the fifth Hadd, the punishment for wine. It says that this consensus is an authority alongside the text.

### The place of exile

The material says that exile can be read as expulsion from the land of Islam, or as expulsion from the place where the crime was committed. It also reports the view of 'Umar al-Faruq that a robber exiled to another town would only harass its people, so it is better to imprison him. The material notes that the Harrah, a place near Madinah, is where the Ukl group were left to die, and it treats their case as the example of how severe the punishment for killing a shepherd and driving off the herd could be.

### In short

- The verse sets out the punishment for armed robbery and rebellion that breaks public peace.
- The four punishments are for the ruler to apply in the way the crime requires, and the material gives the reading of the jurists on that choice.
- The punishment is a disgrace in this world and a greater punishment in the Hereafter, and repentance must include restoring the rights of people.

34.text:
"As for those who repent before you seize them, then know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"

This verse makes an exception to the punishment in 5:33. A robber or rebel who repents before he is taken, while he still has strength and before the authorities have seized him, may be forgiven and the penalty dropped. The verse ends by saying that Allah is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who repent before you seize them."** The material explains that the exception applies only before capture. The robber must abandon the practice while his position of strength still stands, and of his own choice. The material contrasts this with theft and adultery, where a repentant offender who has been proved guilty is not spared the worldly penalty, though his Hereafter punishment may be forgiven.

**"Then know that Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** The material says that the verse's mercy is the reason for the exception. The severity of the punishment for robbery is matched by a door left open for repentance.

### Why the exception exists

The material gives three reasons. First, the robbery punishment falls on the whole group even when one member committed the crime, so the exception softens it. Second, it is not always easy to overcome a powerful group, so the door of persuasion is left open to induce them to repent. Third, killing is an extreme measure, and the law wants it to happen as rarely as possible, so the effort to reform the robbers continues.

The material reports the account of Ali al-Asadi, who waged war and robbed travellers near Madinah, and who repented after a reciter in a caravan recited a verse that tells the servants of Allah not to despair of His mercy. He put down his sword and went to Madinah. Abu Hurayrah took him to Marwan, the governor, and said he could not be punished. Harithah bin Badr also rebelled and then repented, and 'Ali did not impose the legal punishment on him.

### The limit of the exception

The material notes that the exception covers only the worldly punishment for the robbery. It does not return what was taken. Any valuable thing that was taken and still exists must be returned, and where a person was killed or hurt, the family may forgive, or the offender must submit to retaliation. The material says that repentance without restoring the rights of people is incomplete.

### The views of the jurists on the exception

The material gives the views of the jurists on the extent of the exception. Al-Shafi'i held two opinions on the punishment for a robber who has killed and taken property. The more sound of his opinions is that he should be killed and have his limbs cut off on opposite sides, but not crucified. Another opinion is that the crucifixion should be for three days after death, or before the killing. Al-Shafi'i also held that a robber's repentance is of no avail once he has been overpowered by the authorities. The material records that Ibn 'Abbas and al-Shafi'i took the view that the four punishments in 5:33 divide the crimes, so that only the killer is killed, the killer and thief is crucified, the thief alone has his limbs cut off, and the one who only causes fear is banished. Banishment is understood by some to include imprisonment.

Abu Hanifah held that where a robber has been caught before he repents, the repentance excuses him from the worldly punishment, but any money he took must be returned, and the financial liability must be discharged or forgiven.

### The exception and the hudud

The material says that the exception in this verse differs from the general law of the hudud. The phrase "for those who repent" is stated without a further clause to say that the penalty is set aside. Some scholars read this as showing that only the worldly punishment fixed by Allah is waived for the repentant robber, and not the rights of people. The material says this is one reading, and that the scholars did not treat the matter at length before it.

### The case of Marwan and Abu Hurairah

The material gives the account in full. Ali al-Asadi was a robber near Madinah. He heard the verse of not despairing of Allah's mercy from a reciter in a caravan he was attacking, asked him to recite it again, and repented. He went to Madinah, sat with Abu Hurairah in the mosque, and when the people came for him, he said he had come in repentance before they had authority over him. Abu Hurairah took his hand to Marwan bin al-Hakam, the governor of Madinah in the time of Mu'awiyah, and said that he could not be punished. Marwan did not punish him. The material notes that the government was already helpless against this robbery, and that everyone was pleased with the outcome.

The material says that a similar case happened with Harithah bin Badr, who rebelled and then repented and came back to Madinah. 'Ali did not impose the legal punishment on him.

### In short

- A robber who repents before capture, while he still has the upper hand, is excused the worldly punishment.
- The exception softens a severe rule, opens the door to repentance, and keeps killing as rare as possible.
- The exception does not remove the duty to return what was taken or to make amends to those who were harmed.

35.text:
"O believers! Be mindful of Allah and seek what brings you closer to Him and struggle in His Way, so you may be successful"

This verse gives three commands to the believers. They are to fear Allah, to seek the means of nearness to Him, and to strive in His way. The material explains that the verse comes straight after the rules on robbery and the spreading of disorder in 5:33 and 5:34, and before the rule on theft. Between those rules the Qur'an speaks about fear of Allah, worship and striving, and this placement is deliberate. The material reads the verse as a call to the heart before the law is applied to the body.

The material also says that the Qur'an does not simply state a penalty as a cold command. It first softens the heart with the fear of Allah and the Hereafter, so that a person gives up crime from inside. This is why the words of fear of Allah come again and again after the rules of crime and punishment.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers!"** The address is to those who have faith. The material says that the command is for the people who already accept the message, and it asks them to act on what they have accepted.

**"Be mindful of Allah."** The material explains taqwa as fear of Allah that stops a person from crime both in public and in private. It is the one thing that can really hold back a person who is able to act in secret. The verse begins with this because every other command depends on it. Some scholars read taqwa in the wider sense of obeying what Allah commands and keeping away from what He forbids.

**"And seek what brings you closer to Him."** The word wasilah is a means of approach. The material explains that it comes from a root that means to make effort to become close to someone. It is used for the closeness that comes through longing and love. Its meaning is broad. Anything that brings a servant nearer to the one he worships is a wasilah. Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Wa'il, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, 'Ata' and As-Suddi read it as the means of approach. Ibn Zayd gave a similar reading. Qatadah explained it as seeking nearness to Allah by obeying Him and doing what pleases Him. Ibn Jarir reported the same view. The material says that this means seeking nearness through faith and good deeds.

The material also records a hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ described wasilah as a high rank in Paradise, above which there is no rank. It is reported by Jabir bin 'Abdullah in a narration that Al-Bukhari recorded. Muslim recorded that the Prophet ﷺ told the believers to ask for wasilah for him after they answer the adhan, and that whoever does so will earn his intercession. The material says that the highest rank is the Prophet's own, and that every believer may seek it through his love for him. The material also notes that the path to Allah is built on love, and love grows through following the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ. It cites the verse in which Allah says that if people love Him they should follow the Prophet, and that Allah will love them. The more closely a person follows the Sunnah in worship, dealings and conduct, the closer that person comes to Allah.

The material also records that Umar asked Allah for rain in a time of drought through the intercession of al-Abbas, and that the prayer was answered. The Prophet ﷺ taught a blind companion to pray with the Prophet as his wasilah. The material treats these as examples of how a person may ask Allah through the good standing of the righteous.

**"And struggle in His Way."** The material says that jihad is mentioned separately even though it is part of good deeds, to show its higher standing. There is a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that jihad is the highest peak of Islam. The separate mention also answers a possible confusion. The earlier verses forbid spreading disorder on the earth, and jihad could look like disorder to someone who does not understand it. The phrase "in His Way" marks the difference. Robbery and rebellion aim at personal gain. Jihad aims to raise the word of Allah and to end oppression.

**"So you may be successful."** The success promised here is both in this world and the next. The material ties it to the nearness of Allah and to the reward of Paradise, which is a place of comfort and safety for those who strive in His way.

### The wasilah and the believer

The material draws a distinction. The highest rank of guidance belongs in a special way to the Prophet ﷺ, who prayed for it. The lower ranks are open to all believers. The material says that the call to seek the wasilah is therefore a call to every believer to seek nearness through what is commanded. It mentions that the great reformers used the wording of love and longing in this word to show that nearness grows with love for Allah and His Messenger.

### Three steps toward nearness

The material gives a fuller reading of how nearness is reached. It mentions three things that open the way to it: taqwa, good deeds and righteous company. The material says that love of the righteous is also a cause of Allah's pleasure, so that praying to Allah through them is a permitted act. This reading draws on the same report about Umar and al-Abbas.

### In short

- The verse calls the believers to fear Allah, to seek nearness to Him through faith and good deeds, and to strive in His way.
- The wasilah is a means of approach, and its highest form is a rank of Paradise that belongs to the Prophet ﷺ.
- Jihad is named separately to mark its higher standing, and to show that it is not the disorder that the earlier verses forbid.

36.text:
"As for the disbelievers, even if they were to possess everything in the world twice over ˹and offer it all˺ to ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Judgment, it would never be accepted from them. And they will suffer a painful punishment"

This verse describes the fate of those who reject faith. The material says it turns from the call to nearness in the previous verse to the state of those who have turned away from it. The disbelievers are shown offering everything they own, and twice as much, to escape the punishment of the Day of Judgment. It is not accepted from them.

The material says the verse is a warning against kufr and shirk, and against the grip of wealth and worldly desire. It is a rebuke of the greed that takes people away from what is halal and haram, and that keeps them busy with gathering property.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for the disbelievers."** The word kufr means to reject or cover over the truth. The material says that the verse speaks of the rejection of the message. It also refers to shirk, the joining of partners with Allah in His divinity. Both states are named because both cut a person off from the way of nearness.

**"Even if they were to possess everything in the world twice over."** The material explains that the picture is of a person who owns all the wealth of the earth, and then the same again. The image is chosen to show that no amount of wealth can buy a release from the punishment.

**"To ransom themselves from the punishment of the Day of Judgment."** The material says that a ransom is something given in exchange for freedom. On the Day of Judgment, there is no exchange of this kind. The verse says that no ransom will be accepted. The material also says that a disbeliever will be certain of the punishment, and will not be able to evade it.

**"It would never be accepted from them."** The phrase is final. The material explains that the punishment is not lifted by any payment. The door of repentance is closed at that point, because the time for acting in this world has passed.

**"And they will suffer a painful punishment."** The punishment is described as painful. The material says that this is a punishment of pain and not only of fear, and that it is the lasting result of a life spent in heedlessness.

### The rebuke of gathering wealth

The material explains that people often commit sins in order to meet their own needs and those of their families. Because wealth brings comfort, they seek it without distinguishing between what is halal and what is haram. The verse shows that this search is empty in the end. Comfort gained in a short life is never enough, and more always follows. This race for gold and greed comes to an end on the Day of Judgment, when the wealth cannot be used. The material says that the verse is a cure for this condition. Once a person understands that wealth cannot buy him out of the punishment, he has a reason to turn away from sin.

### In short

- Those who reject the truth and join partners with Allah cannot escape the punishment by offering wealth.
- The verse uses the image of double wealth to show how complete the loss is.
- The greed for wealth that makes people indifferent to halal and haram is what the verse warns against.

37.text:
"They will be desperate to get out of the Fire but they will never be able to. And they will suffer an everlasting punishment"

This verse completes the picture of the fate of the disbelievers. The material says it describes their state in the Fire. They long to leave, but they cannot.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They will be desperate to get out of the Fire."** The material explains that the word for desperate describes a longing that is full of anguish. The people in the Fire will want to leave, because the pain is severe. The material says that every time the flames lift them toward the upper parts of Hell, the angels of punishment strike them with iron bars and drive them back down.

**"But they will never be able to."** The denial is firm. The material says that there is no way out, and no means of escape or self-rescue.

**"And they will suffer an everlasting punishment."** The material says that this punishment is eternal, and that the people in it will never depart from it or avoid it. The verse is read alongside a hadith reported by Anas bin Malik and recorded by Muslim and An-Nasa'i. In it, a man from the people of the Fire is asked whether he would ransom himself with the earth's fill of gold. He says yes. Allah tells him that he was asked for less and did not do it, and he is ordered into the Fire.

### In short

- The people of the Fire long to leave, but they are driven back and cannot escape.
- The punishment is everlasting, and no ransom or wish can change it.
- The hadith of Anas shows that a request for a smaller thing in this world, once refused, leads to the Fire.

38.text:
"As for male and female thieves, cut off their hands for what they have done—a deterrent from Allah. And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise"

This verse sets out the punishment for theft. The material places it among the Hudud, the punishments that the Qur'an itself fixes and that no ruler may change. The verse follows the rules on robbery in 5:33 and 5:34, and it moves from the crime against the road to the crime against property taken in secret. The material notes that the rule is stated as the right of Allah, which is why it is called the Hadd of Sariqah, the punishment for theft.

The material also explains that the rule is harsh only in its outline. Its application is bounded by many conditions, so that in practice the hand is cut off only in a narrow set of cases.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for male and female thieves."** The material notes that the Qur'an normally addresses men, and that women are understood to be included. In the matter of theft and adultery the text names both sexes separately. The reason given is that a Hadd may be dropped on the slightest doubt, so the Qur'an leaves nothing implied. The material also notes that in the verse on adultery in 24:2 the order is reversed, with the woman first. The reason given there is that a man who steals has many lawful ways to earn, so his theft is the graver fault, while a woman is protected by her natural modesty and by the people around her.

**"Cut off their hands."** The material explains that the cut is made at the wrist, and that the right hand is the one taken. The Sunnah describes a further penalty for repeat offences, with the left foot, then the left hand and the right foot, after which a discretionary punishment applies.

**"For what they have done."** The word translated as the reward is a requital. The material says that the hand is cut because it was the tool used to take what belonged to others. It is fitting that the tool of the wrong is the part that is punished.

**"A deterrent from Allah."** The Arabic word is nakal, a punishment that serves as a lesson to others and holds them back. The material says that the rule is meant to remove the crime from society by making an example of the offender. The phrase "from Allah" marks a second aspect of the crime. Theft is an injustice to the victim, and it is also an act against the command of Allah. Because of the second aspect, the punishment is a Hadd and not a Qisas, a crime against the public order. The victim cannot forgive it, and only Allah can.

**"And Allah is Almighty, All-Wise."** The material reads this closing phrase as an answer to those who call the rule savage. It says that the severity of the rule belongs to the mighty and wise will of Allah, and that its purpose is also wise.

### The limits of the rule

The material sets out the conditions for the Hadd of theft. The first condition is that the property belongs to someone privately. If the thief has a share in it, or if there is doubt about ownership, or if it is shared by the public, the Hadd does not apply. The second condition is that the property is kept in a secure place, such as a locked house or a guarded store. Property left in the open is not covered. A doubt about security also removes the Hadd. The third condition is that the thief has no permission to take the item. A person who was allowed to enter the house and take an item does not fall under the Hadd, even if he steals. The fourth condition is that the theft is done in secret. Open seizure is robbery, which has its own rules.

The material gives examples of thefts that do not carry the Hadd. Items taken from public places such as a mosque, a park or a station are not in a secure place. Fruit hanging on trees and honey are not covered. Pickpocketing, snatching, fraud and breach of trust are all unlawful, but they are punished by a discretionary penalty. Stealing from a grave is also unlawful, but the shroud is not owned by the dead, so the Hadd does not apply. A theft from property held in joint ownership is also not covered, because the thief has a share.

### The minimum value and the hadith

The material gives the hadith on the value of stolen goods, which is the basis for the minimum. Abu Hurayrah reported a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that cursed the thief who steals an egg or a rope and loses his hand over it. A'ishah reported, in the two sahihs and in Muslim's collection, that the hand is cut off only when the theft reaches a quarter of a dinar or more. The material says this hadith fixes the value. Some reports give three dirhams, and the material reconciles them, since a dinar then equalled twelve dirhams, so three dirhams were a quarter of a dinar.

The material records that this view was held by Umar bin al-Khattab, Uthman bin Affan and Ali bin Abi Talib. It also records that Umar bin Abdul-Aziz, al-Layth bin Sa'd, al-Awza'i and Ash-Shafi'i held it, with his companions. Ahmad bin Hanbal and Ishaq bin Rahwayh in one narration, and Abu Thawr, also held it. Dawud al-Zahiri took the same view. The material records that Abu Hanifah and his students Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Zufar, and Sufyan Ath-Thawri, held that the minimum is ten dirhams. The material prefers the first view as the sounder one, and it says the low limit was set so that people would refrain from theft.

### The woman, the ransom and Makkah

The material says the story of the woman from Makhzum took place during the conquest of Makkah. Az-Zuhri reported it from Urwah from A'ishah, and the two sahihs record it. The Quraysh feared for the woman and sent Usamah, the beloved of the Prophet ﷺ, to speak for her. This is the same narration that is set out in the entry for verse 38 above.

### The Hudud as the law of the land

The material says that the Hudud are part of Islamic law, the shariah, and that the fiqh of the Hudud is set out in the Hanafi books of jurisprudence. It notes that the Hadd of theft is a Hadd and that its conditions are bound up with the rules of the ruler and the judge. The material also notes that the same law governs acts of worship such as salah, sawm, hajj and zakah, but in the case of theft and adultery the Qur'an names both sexes, because the Hadd must be applied only in clear cases.

### Repentance and the path to Allah

The material links repentance here with the path that leads to Allah. Taqwa is the fear of Allah that keeps a person from crime. Jihad is the struggle against the self and against wrong. The material says that a thief who gives up his sin and corrects his life is treading the path back to Allah, and that the path is open to anyone who turns to Him.

### The law of evidence

The material explains that the proof required for a Hadd is stricter than for other matters. For theft two male witnesses are needed, and their testimony must be given promptly. A witness who gives evidence after a long delay is not accepted. The judge cannot accept the testimony of a person known to sin in a Hadd case, even when he might accept it in other matters. Where the proof is incomplete, the punishment falls to the discretionary level.

The material says that the outcome of these conditions is that the Hadd is applied only rarely, because the crime and its proof must both be complete. In the cases where both are found, the punishment is severe, and it serves as a warning that discourages others from the same act.

### The tradition of the woman from Makhzum

The material gives the account that Ahmad, Abdullah bin 'Amr and the two sahihs record in various forms. A woman from the tribe of Makhzum stole during the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Her people asked for a ransom, and the Prophet ﷺ refused and ordered the hand cut off. She asked whether repentance was open to her, and he told her that she was free of her sin that day. The verse on repentance in 5:39 was then revealed. The matter became a concern to the Quraysh, who asked Usamah to intercede. The Prophet ﷺ said that intercession in a punishment prescribed by Allah is not permitted, and he gave a speech in which he warned that earlier nations fell because they punished the weak and let the powerful go. He said that if Fatimah had stolen he would have cut her hand off. A'ishah reported that the woman repented sincerely, married, and came to her with her needs.

### The modern objection

The material responds to those who call the Hudud harsh. It says that in the places where the Hudud are applied, the number of thefts is low, and that shops are left open without fear. It reads the rule as an act of mercy to the many, and it says that showing mercy to a criminal can be cruelty to society. The material also contrasts this with the position of those who object to these rules while holding weapons that have killed many civilians. It adds that God revealed the Hudud alongside the instruction to not show mercy in enforcing them, and that the law of retaliation is described as a life for those who understand. The material ends with a prayer that such people may be guided to the true path of peace.

### In short

- The verse sets out the cutting of the hand for theft as a Hadd, a right of Allah and a deterrent.
- The rule applies only when strict conditions are met, including secure property, private ownership, no permission and secret taking.
- The proof is strictly required, and any doubt replaces the Hadd with a discretionary punishment.

39.text:
"But whoever repents after their wrongdoing and mends their ways, Allah will surely turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful"

This verse follows the rule on theft and opens a door of repentance. The material compares it with the exception in 5:34 for those who repent before the robbers are taken. The two verses use forgiveness in different ways.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But whoever repents after their wrongdoing and mends their ways."** The material explains that repentance here is a turning away from the sin and a correction of conduct. It is not enough to say sorry. The person must stop stealing and make right what he has done.

**"Allah will surely turn to them in forgiveness."** The material says that this forgiveness is in the Hereafter. A thief who repents is forgiven by Allah from the punishment of the next life. The forgiveness does not remove the worldly Hadd. Once the crime is proved before a judge, the ruler cannot drop the punishment because of repentance.

**"Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** The material links this to the verse on the power of Allah in 2:284, which says He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.

### The difference from the robbery exception

The material explains that the exception in 5:34 applies to the worldly punishment. A robber who repents before he is overpowered is excused the Hadd. The thief in 5:39 is treated differently. Repentance does not stop the hand from being cut, once the case is proved. It does bring deliverance in the Hereafter. Most jurists agree that the Hadd for robbery is not applied to a robber who repents before arrest. For theft, the material says that a thief who repents after the theft, whether before or after arrest, still faces the Hadd. This is the reading of al-Shafi'i, who held that a thief pardoned before being brought to the ruler escapes the amputation. The material records that once the matter has reached the ruler, the victim's right to restitution and the Hadd remain.

### The path back and the schools

The material says that a person who repents has taken the path of taqwa, which is the fear of Allah, and of jihad, which is the struggle against his own desires. The path is open to any thief who gives up his theft and corrects himself. The material notes that Ash-Shafi'i and other jurists held that a thief who is pardoned before he reaches the ruler escapes the Hadd. The hadith on the egg and the rope, which is recorded by Abu Hurayrah, and the report of A'ishah in Muslim, are the points on which the schools rest their views on value.

### In short

- Repentance and correction bring forgiveness from Allah in the Hereafter.
- Repentance does not stop the worldly Hadd for theft once the case is proved.
- The verse is read against the exception in 5:34, which does excuse the robber who repents before capture.

40.text:
"Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah ˹alone˺? He punishes whoever He wills and forgives whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything"

This verse closes the passage on theft and robbery. It states that Allah alone owns the heavens and the earth, and that He alone decides who is punished and who is forgiven. The material reads it as a reply to those who think that the Hudud violate human dignity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Do you not know that the kingdom of the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah alone?"** The question is an affirmation. The material says that the owner of all things is the one who sets the law. Human judgement is therefore bounded by His command.

**"He punishes whoever He wills and forgives whoever He wills."** The material says that punishment and forgiveness both come from the wisdom of Allah. It cites the verse in 2:284 that gives the same pattern.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything."** The power of Allah reaches all things, including punishment and forgiveness. The material says that the limits of His wisdom cannot be measured by human reason, but enough of it is open to human understanding to bring peace to the heart.

### The Hudud and the modern objection

The material gives a full account of the five Hudud. The punishment for robbery is the cutting of the right hand and left foot. For theft it is the cutting of the right hand at the wrist. For adultery it is a hundred lashes, or stoning in some cases. For false accusation of adultery it is eighty lashes. For drinking wine it is eighty lashes, by the consensus of the Companions. All other offences are left to the discretion of the ruler and the judge, who may set penalties in line with the crime and the circumstances. The material says that in many modern systems the law is passed by an assembly and the judges apply it within set limits.

Even for the five Hudud, the material says, the punishment is not applied where the proof is missing or the conditions are incomplete. In those cases a discretionary penalty is given instead. The benefit of any doubt goes to the accused. The result is that the Hadd is rare and that most cases end in discretionary punishment.

The material gives examples of how strict the definition of theft is. Taking from public places, from trees, or from a house where one was permitted to enter does not meet the definition. Pickpocketing and fraud are punished, but not by amputation. The material notes that the Hadd is not applied when the thief has a share in the property. It adds that in such cases, the conditions of security and permission and proof are all considered before the Hadd can apply.

The material also argues that a society where crime is punished severely can be more peaceful than one where criminals are treated gently, and it offers the example of certain places where the Hudud are applied and shops are left open without fear. It addresses the objection that these punishments are savage by comparing them with the conduct of states that have built and stored weapons of mass destruction. It says that deterrence works in both cases, and it asks why what human beings can do in their own interest cannot be done by God in His wisdom. The material ends with a prayer that those who oppose Islamic punishments may be guided to the true way of peace.

### The shariah, fiqh and the Hudud in Makkah

The material explains that the shariah rules for the five Hudud are set in the fiqh books. It notes that Makkah, Madinah and the lands of the early Muslims had rules that followed the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and that the Hajj and Umrah bring Muslims from many countries to see these rules in practice. Many who have visited report that shops are left open during the prayer times, and that owners leave their stock without fear of loss. The material says that the Hudud are the reason for that order, and it argues that this order is a benefit to the whole community, not only to the thief who would otherwise be shown mercy.

### The consensus on wine

The material records the consensus of the Companions on the fifth Hadd, the eighty lashes for wine. It says that this consensus, like the Qur'an, is a source of law, and that the other four Hudud were fixed by the text itself.

### The rules of the Hadd of theft in the fiqh

The material notes that the jurists who wrote on the Hadd of theft, including the authors of the Hanafi jurisprudence, set the conditions in detail. The rules of the Hadd are stated in a way that makes the Hadd rare, and this is in keeping with the wisdom of the shariah. The material says that the crime and the proof must both be complete, and that any doubt causes the Hadd to be replaced by a discretionary punishment.

### In short

- Allah owns the heavens and the earth, and His power and wisdom govern punishment and forgiveness.
- The five Hudud are fixed by the text or by consensus, and all other offences are left to the judge.
- The strict conditions for the Hadd of theft mean that it is applied rarely, and the material defends it as a deterrent that protects the public.

41.text:
"O Messenger! Do not grieve for those who race to disbelieve—those who say, “We believe” with their tongues, but their hearts are in disbelief. Nor those among the Jews who eagerly listen to lies, attentive to those who are too arrogant to come to you. They distort the Scripture, taking rulings out of context, then say, “If this is the ruling you get ˹from Muḥammad˺, accept it. If not, beware!” Whoever Allah allows to be deluded, you can never be of any help to them against Allah. It is not Allah’s Will to purify their hearts. For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter"

This verse is a word of comfort to the Prophet ﷺ and a warning to the believers. It describes a group of hypocrites who showed a Muslim face in Madinah, and a group of Jews who listened to the Prophet ﷺ in order to carry his words back to their leaders. The material says the verse opens the next part of the chapter, which returns to the People of the Book after a short break. Its subject is the Jewish tribes who lived near Madinah, and the cases they brought to the Prophet ﷺ.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O Messenger! Do not grieve."** The address is one of consolation. The material explains that the Prophet ﷺ was grieved by those who rushed to reject the message. The verse tells him that their rejection is not his failure, and that he is not responsible for their hearts.

**"Those who race to disbelieve."** The material reads this as a description of those who hurry toward kufr, the rejection of the truth. They are described as racing because they do not hesitate to reject it, and they seek out every opportunity to do so.

**"Those who say, 'We believe,' with their tongues, but their hearts are in disbelief."** The material identifies these as the hypocrites. It says that the hypocrites professed faith in words while their hearts held no faith at all. Ibn Ubayy and his followers are named in the material as the leaders of this group. The grammar of the verse ties "with their tongues" to the word "say," so the claim of faith is spoken and not believed.

**"Nor those among the Jews who eagerly listen to lies."** The material says that the Jews are described as listeners who are eager to hear falsehood. The verse does not say they hear the truth. It says they gather falsehood and bring it back with them. The material mentions Banu Qurayzah and Ka'b and his followers as the Jewish side of the group.

**"Attentive to those who are too arrogant to come to you."** The material explains that the more prominent among them refused to come to the Prophet ﷺ in person, out of pride. They sent inferiors to listen to him, and those inferiors carried his words to their leaders. The material says that this is why the verse speaks of listeners on behalf of others.

**"They distort the Scripture, taking rulings out of context."** The material explains the phrase as the changing of words from their places, by altering their meanings after they have understood them. The Torah is the Scripture in view. The material says the change was made knowingly.

**"If this is the ruling you get from Muhammad, accept it. If not, beware!"** The material reports that this was said by the leaders to their followers. The sense is that the followers should accept the Prophet's ruling only if it suits them, and should reject it if it does not.

**"Whoever Allah allows to be deluded, you can never be of any help to them against Allah."** The material explains that no one can protect a person whom Allah has left in his delusion. It notes that a trial can mean a test, and that the verse is saying the Prophet ﷺ cannot save such people by his own effort.

**"It is not Allah's Will to purify their hearts."** The material explains that the purification of the heart means cleansing from treachery, scheming and persistence in kufr. It says that these people have shut themselves out of this purification by their own choice.

**"For them is disgrace in this world, and they will suffer a tremendous punishment in the Hereafter."** The material explains the disgrace as humiliation in this world, and the Hereafter punishment as greater than the worldly one. It notes that the Jewish tribes were later made to suffer for their conduct.

### The background of the verse

The material explains that the verse grew out of two cases between the Jewish tribes near Madinah. The first concerned killing and retaliation, and the second concerned adultery and its punishment.

Before Islam, the tribes of Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir lived near Madinah. Banu Nadir were the stronger and wealthier. They forced Banu Qurayzah into a harsh agreement on the blood money for killing. If a man of Banu Nadir killed a man of Banu Qurayzah, there was no retaliation, and only a payment of dates was due. If a man of Banu Qurayzah killed a man of Banu Nadir, the killer was put to death and a larger payment was taken. The material lists other unequal terms, such as two men of Banu Qurayzah being killed for one of Banu Nadir, and two hands or ears being taken for one. Banu Qurayzah were too weak to refuse.

When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, these tribes had not become Muslims and were not bound by any treaty with the Muslim community. The material says that they still knew the Torah pointed to the Last Prophet. They used the Islamic principle of equality as a support in their dispute with Banu Nadir. Banu Qurayzah refused to pay the doubled blood money, and Banu Nadir threatened war. The two sides agreed to take the case to the Prophet ﷺ. The material says Banu Nadir then sent a delegation of their hypocritical allies to learn his judgement before he gave it. These men were told to accept his ruling only if it favoured Banu Nadir.

The material gives a second case, from Khaybar. A married couple from a noble Jewish family had committed adultery. The Torah prescribed stoning, but their people hoped for a lighter punishment. They sent the couple to Banu Qurayzah, asking them to bring the case to Muhammad, with the same condition: accept the ruling if it is light, reject it if it is heavy.

### The Torah and the verse of stoning

The material gives the account of the Jewish adulterers, which Al-Bukhari and Muslim record. It was reported by Ibn 'Umar, who said that the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him that a man and a woman among them had committed adultery. He asked what the Torah says about stoning. They said it prescribes only exposure and flogging. Abdullah bin Salam said they were lying, and that the Torah mentions stoning. The reader hid the verse with his hand, but when Abdullah bin Salam told him to remove it, the verse on stoning was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ ordered the two to be stoned. Ibn 'Umar said that he was among those who stoned them, and that he saw the man shielding the woman from the stones with his body.

The material gives another report from Abu Dawud, in which the Prophet ﷺ sat on the Torah, placed it on the pillow, and said that he trusted it and the One who revealed it. He asked for their most learned man. The material also gives a report from al-Bara' bin Azib, who said that the Jewish man had been flogged and darkened with coal, and that the Prophet ﷺ asked a Jewish scholar to confirm the Torah's rule. The scholar said the Torah prescribes stoning, but that the notables had stopped it and replaced it with flogging and blackening the face. The Prophet ﷺ said that he was the first to bring back the command that had been suspended, and he ordered the Jewish man to be stoned.

The material explains that the Prophet ﷺ asked them about the Torah not out of honour for their book, but because Allah commanded him to do so. It made them admit what they had hidden. Their coming to him was motivated by desire, hoping for a lighter punishment, and not by belief in his judgement.

### The judicial process for non-Muslims

The material explains that these Jews were not Dhimmis of the Islamic state, nor did they believe in its law. They had a pact of no war with the Prophet ﷺ. Because of this, he had the choice to turn away or to judge between them. Abu Bakr al-Jassas, in his work on the rulings of the Qur'an, reconciled the two verses on this point. The choice in the verse applies to people who are under a pact but are not citizens. The command to judge applies to citizens of the Islamic state, who owe allegiance to its law.

The material says that in either case the Prophet ﷺ judged according to the law revealed by Allah, and not according to the desires of the parties. In matters of common law, such as the punishment for killing or adultery, the rule is the same for everyone. The material gives the example of the hand of the thief, which applies to all citizens. But personal and religious matters of non-Muslims are left to their own religion. The Prophet ﷺ did not interfere with the marriages of the Magians, the Jews and the Christians, and he accepted them as valid. When non-Muslim citizens bring a case to a Muslim judge by agreement, the judge rules by his own law.

### The four traits of the group

The material ends its explanation with four evil traits of the group the verse describes. The first is to race toward disbelief. The second is to listen eagerly to lies. The third is to distort the Scripture from its context. The fourth is to put personal desire above the command of Allah. The material says that the Muslim is warned against these traits, and that they reject the truth.

The material also draws a broader lesson. A person who places his personal interests above the truth, and who distorts the message to justify himself, loses the capacity to accept the truth. The servant of Allah who carries the message should not be discouraged by opposition, because the efforts of opponents are not against the messenger but against Allah, and so they cannot succeed.

### The reports on the reason for the verse

The material gives several accounts of the reason for revelation. Some say it was revealed about the hypocrites and the Jews, and the subject of the blood money. Others say it was about the adulterers of Khaybar. The material says that Ibn 'Abbas, Al-Bara' bin Azib, Hudhayfah bin Al-Yaman, Abu Mijlaz, 'Ikrimah and Al-Hasan Al-Basri all held that the verse concerned the People of the Book, and that Al-Hasan added that it applies to the Muslims as well. The material also reports that Ibrahim and Mansur took the verses as applying to the Children of Israel, and that Allah accepted them for this Ummah.

The material says that the verses on the rulings in this chapter are related to these events, and that the lesson of the verse is clear. Its language is a comfort to the Prophet ﷺ, a warning to the believers, and a judgement on those who used the Scripture to suit their desires.

### In short

- The verse comforts the Prophet ﷺ and warns against the hypocrites and Jews who used his words for their own purposes.
- It describes two cases, the blood money of Banu Qurayzah and Banu Nadir and the adultery of the Jewish couple, and shows how the Torah's stoning rule came back to light.
- Judgement under a pact or for citizens follows the law of Allah, and the traits the verse names must be avoided by the believer.

42.text:
"They eagerly listen to falsehood and consume forbidden gain. So if they come to you ˹O Prophet˺, either judge between them or turn away from them. If you turn away from them, they cannot harm you whatsoever. But if you judge between them, then do so with justice. Surely Allah loves those who are just"

This verse continues the description of the Jewish listeners who came to the Prophet ﷺ. It names two faults, listening to falsehood and taking forbidden gain. It then gives the Prophet ﷺ the choice to judge between them or to turn away, and sets the condition for judging, which is justice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"They eagerly listen to falsehood."** The material explains that these are people who are used to listening to what is false and going along with it. They hear lies from their leaders, and they keep following them even when those leaders openly deny the Torah. The material says this is the first trait the verse names.

**"And consume forbidden gain."** The Arabic word is suht, which the material explains as bribery. The root sense is destruction, but here it means money taken unlawfully. The material cites the hadith that Allah curses the giver and the taker of a bribe and the broker between them. The material gives a legal definition: taking payment for a duty that one is already bound to perform. A judge, a clerk or a father who is paid for a marriage that is his duty all fall under it. The Qur'an treats such gain as forbidden.

**"So if they come to you, either judge between them or turn away from them."** The material says the choice was given first. Some scholars held that this choice was later replaced by the command in 5:49 to judge between them. Al-Shafi'i held one of his two opinions on this point. The material says that if the parties ask for arbitration from a Muslim judge, he is bound to judge between them. If a Muslim is one of the parties, the judge is bound by the consensus of the jurists, not by al-Shafi'i alone.

**"If you turn away from them, they cannot harm you whatsoever."** The material says that the Prophet ﷺ was not harmed by their refusal, since their hearts were already closed to him and their aim was to find a verdict that suited them.

**"But if you judge between them, then do so with justice."** The material notes that justice is required even if the Jews were unfair and were enemies of the Muslims.
